INV-03.KOSPI: The Korea Composite Stock Price Index, which tracks the common stocks on the main board of South Korea's stock exchange.
INV-03.ASX 200: Tracks 200 of the largest companies on the Australian Securities Exchange. It is the main index for Australia.
INV-03.IBEX 35: Tracks 35 of the most heavily traded companies on the Madrid stock exchange. It is the main index for Spain.
INV-03.Dow Jones Transportation Average: Tracks 20 U.S. transportation companies, such as airlines, railroads and trucking firms. It is the oldest U.S. stock index.

INV-04.New York Stock Exchange: The world's largest stock exchange by the value of its listed companies, based on Wall Street in New York City.
INV-04.Nasdaq: A fully electronic U.S. exchange based in New York, known for listing many technology companies.
INV-04.London Stock Exchange: The main stock exchange of the United Kingdom and one of the oldest in the world.
INV-04.Tokyo Stock Exchange: Japan's main stock exchange and one of the largest in Asia. It is run by Japan Exchange Group.
INV-04.Shanghai Stock Exchange: The larger of mainland China's two main stock exchanges, home to many big state-owned companies.
INV-04.Hong Kong Stock Exchange: The stock exchange of Hong Kong, where many large Chinese companies list to reach international investors.
INV-04.Toronto Stock Exchange: Canada's main stock exchange, known for its many mining, energy and banking companies.
INV-04.Euronext: A European exchange group that runs the stock markets in several cities, including Paris, Amsterdam, Brussels, Lisbon, Dublin, Oslo and Milan.
INV-04.Frankfurt Stock Exchange: Germany's main stock exchange, operated by Deutsche Boerse.
INV-04.Bombay Stock Exchange: A stock exchange in Mumbai, India, and the oldest in Asia. It is now known as BSE.
INV-04.Cboe: A U.S. exchange operator that began as the Chicago Board Options Exchange. It is best known for options and also runs stock exchanges.
INV-04.Shenzhen Stock Exchange: The second of mainland China's two main stock exchanges, known for smaller and more technology-focused companies.
INV-04.National Stock Exchange of India: India's largest stock exchange by trading volume, based in Mumbai. It was the country's first fully electronic exchange.
INV-04.Australian Securities Exchange: Australia's main stock exchange, based in Sydney.
INV-04.NYSE American: A U.S. exchange for smaller companies, owned by the New York Stock Exchange's parent. It was formerly the American Stock Exchange.
INV-04.NYSE Chicago: The name the Chicago Stock Exchange, a regional U.S. exchange dating from the 1880s, took after the New York Stock Exchange's parent bought it. In 2025 it was renamed NYSE Texas.
INV-04.IEX: Investors Exchange, a U.S. stock exchange known for a tiny built-in delay on orders, designed to blunt the advantage of high-speed traders.
INV-04.Korea Exchange: South Korea's stock exchange. Its main office is in Busan and its main trading market is in Seoul.
INV-04.Singapore Exchange: The stock and derivatives exchange of Singapore.
INV-04.SIX Swiss Exchange: Switzerland's main stock exchange, based in Zurich.
INV-04.Johannesburg Stock Exchange: South Africa's stock exchange and the largest in Africa.
INV-04.B3 Brazil: Brazil's stock exchange, based in Sao Paulo. It was formed from a merger that included the older Bovespa exchange.
INV-04.Mexican Stock Exchange: Mexico's main stock exchange, based in Mexico City. Its Spanish name is Bolsa Mexicana de Valores.
INV-04.Taiwan Stock Exchange: The main stock exchange of Taiwan, based in Taipei and home to many electronics and chip makers.
INV-04.Saudi Exchange: Saudi Arabia's stock exchange, also known as Tadawul. It is the largest in the Middle East.
INV-04.Borsa Italiana: Italy's stock exchange, based in Milan. It is now part of the Euronext group.
INV-04.Moscow Exchange: Russia's largest exchange, where stocks, bonds and currencies are traded.
INV-04.Nasdaq PHLX: The former Philadelphia Stock Exchange, the oldest stock exchange in the U.S. It is now owned by Nasdaq and trades mainly options.

INV-05.Treasury bond: A long-term loan to the U.S. government, with a life of 20 or 30 years. It pays interest every six months and is considered very safe.
INV-05.Corporate bond: A loan to a company. It usually pays more interest than a similar government bond because there is more risk the company will not repay.
INV-05.Municipal bond: A bond issued by a state, city or other local government to fund public projects. Its interest is usually free of federal income tax.
INV-05.Savings bond: A bond the U.S. government sells directly to individuals. It builds up interest over time and cannot be sold to another investor.
INV-05.Junk bond: A bond from an issuer with a low credit rating. It pays a higher interest rate to make up for the greater chance of default.
INV-05.Treasury note or bill: Shorter U.S. government debt. Bills mature in a year or less and are sold at a discount. Notes run 2 to 10 years and pay interest twice a year.
INV-05.Zero-coupon bond: A bond that pays no regular interest. It is sold well below face value, and the investor's return is the full face value paid at maturity.
INV-05.Convertible bond: A corporate bond the holder can swap for a set number of the company's shares instead of waiting to be repaid in cash.
INV-05.Coupon bond: A bond that pays a fixed amount of interest, called the coupon, at regular intervals until it matures.
INV-05.TIPS: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities. These U.S. government bonds adjust their principal with inflation, so the investor's buying power is protected.
INV-05.Callable bond: A bond the issuer has the right to repay early, before the maturity date. Issuers usually do this when interest rates have fallen.
INV-05.Agency bond: A bond issued by a U.S. government agency or a government-sponsored company such as Fannie Mae, often to support home lending.
INV-05.Investment-grade bond: A bond rated in the top tiers by credit rating agencies, meaning the issuer is judged likely to repay.
INV-05.Foreign bond: A bond issued by a government or company from another country. It can carry extra currency and political risk.
INV-05.Mortgage-backed security: A bond-like investment built from a pool of home loans. Investors receive the homeowners' interest and principal payments.
INV-05.Revenue bond: A municipal bond repaid only from the income of the project it funds, such as tolls from a bridge or fees from a water system.
INV-05.General obligation bond: A municipal bond backed by the full taxing power of the government that issues it, not by one project's income.
INV-05.Debenture: A bond backed only by the issuer's general credit and reputation, with no specific property pledged as security.
INV-05.Secured bond: A bond backed by specific assets, such as property or equipment, that bondholders can claim if the issuer fails to pay.
INV-05.Floating-rate bond: A bond whose interest payments rise and fall with a benchmark interest rate instead of staying fixed.
INV-05.Green bond: A bond whose proceeds are set aside for environmental projects, such as renewable energy or clean transport.
INV-05.Serial or term bond: Two ways to schedule repayment. Serial bonds from one issue mature in stages over several years. Term bonds all mature on one date.
INV-05.Bearer or registered bond: A registered bond records the owner's name with the issuer. A bearer bond belongs to whoever holds the paper, and is now rare.
INV-05.Putable bond: A bond the investor has the right to sell back to the issuer before maturity at a set price, useful if interest rates rise.
INV-05.Perpetual bond: A bond with no maturity date. It pays interest indefinitely and the principal is never scheduled to be repaid.

INS-01.Premium: The amount you pay, usually monthly or yearly, to keep an insurance policy in force.
INS-01.Deductible: The amount you must pay toward a covered loss yourself before the insurer starts paying.
INS-01.Claim: A formal request asking the insurer to pay for a loss that the policy covers.
INS-01.Coverage: The protection a policy provides, meaning the kinds of loss the insurer has agreed to pay for.
INS-01.Copay: A fixed amount you pay for a health service, such as a doctor visit or prescription, with the insurer paying the rest.
INS-01.Policy: The written contract between you and the insurer that sets out what is covered, for how much and at what price.
INS-01.Coverage limit: The most the insurer will pay for a covered loss. Costs above that amount are your responsibility.
INS-01.Beneficiary: The person or organization named to receive the money from a policy, most often a life insurance payout.
INS-01.Policyholder: The person or business that owns the policy and is protected by it.
INS-01.Insurer: The company that sells the policy and promises to pay for covered losses.
INS-01.Benefits: The payments or services the insurer provides under the policy when a covered event happens.
INS-01.Coinsurance: The percentage of a covered cost you pay after meeting the deductible, with the insurer paying the remaining share.
INS-01.Exclusions: Losses or situations the policy specifically says it will not pay for, such as flood damage under a standard home policy.
INS-01.Out-of-pocket maximum: The most you will have to pay for covered health care in a year. After you reach it, the insurer pays all covered costs.
INS-01.Agent: A person licensed to sell insurance policies and help customers with their coverage.
INS-01.Network: The doctors, hospitals and other providers that have agreed prices with a health insurer. Using them usually costs you less.
INS-01.Risk: The chance that a loss will happen. Insurance exists to shift the financial cost of that chance from you to the insurer.
INS-01.Rider: An add-on that changes a standard policy, usually by adding coverage, often for an extra cost.
INS-01.Grace period: A short time after a premium is due when you can still pay and keep the policy from being canceled.
INS-01.Policy period: The span of time, from the start date to the end date, during which the policy's coverage applies.
INS-01.Peril: A specific cause of loss, such as fire, theft or wind. A policy lists which ones it covers.
INS-01.Actual cash value: What damaged property was worth just before the loss, meaning the cost to replace it minus depreciation for age and wear.
INS-01.Replacement cost: The cost of replacing damaged property with a new item of similar kind, with nothing taken off for age or wear.
INS-01.Face value: The amount a life insurance policy promises to pay when the insured person dies. It is stated on the policy.
INS-01.Cash value: The savings portion that builds up inside a permanent life insurance policy. The owner can borrow against it or take it on canceling.
INS-01.Underwriting: The process an insurer uses to judge how risky an applicant is, then decide whether to offer coverage and at what price.
INS-01.Adjuster: The person who investigates a claim and works out how much the insurer should pay.
INS-01.Pre-existing condition: A health problem a person already had before their coverage started.
INS-01.Renewal: Continuing a policy for another term when the current one ends, often with an updated premium.
INS-01.Declarations page: The first page of a policy. It sums up who and what is insured, the coverage limits, the deductibles and the premium.
INS-01.Insuring agreement: The part of the policy where the insurer states what it promises to cover and pay.
INS-01.Indemnity: The principle that insurance should restore you to the financial position you were in before the loss, with no profit from it.
INS-01.Subrogation: The insurer's right, after paying your claim, to recover that money from the person who caused the loss.
INS-01.Insurable interest: A real financial stake in the person or property insured. To buy coverage, you must be someone who would lose money if the loss happened.
INS-01.Lapse: The ending of coverage because the premium was not paid.
INS-01.Waiting period: A set time that must pass after coverage begins, or after a loss, before benefits start being paid.
INS-01.Hazard: A condition that makes a loss more likely or more severe, such as icy roads or faulty wiring.
INS-01.Conditions: The section setting out the rules both sides must follow, such as reporting a loss promptly, for coverage to apply.

INS-02.Liability: Pays for injuries to other people and damage to their property when you cause an accident. Nearly every state requires it.
INS-02.Collision: Pays to repair or replace your own car after it hits another vehicle or an object, whoever was at fault.
INS-02.Comprehensive: Pays for damage to your car from causes other than a crash, such as theft, fire, hail, vandalism or hitting an animal.
INS-02.Uninsured motorist: Pays your costs when you are hit by a driver who has no insurance, or by one whose insurance is too small to cover the damage.
INS-02.Medical payments: Pays medical bills for you and your passengers after an accident, whoever was at fault.
INS-02.Personal injury protection: Pays medical bills, and often lost wages, for you and your passengers whoever caused the accident. No-fault states require it.
INS-02.Roadside assistance: Pays for help when your car breaks down, such as a tow, a jump-start, a flat tire change or a lockout service.
INS-02.Rental reimbursement: Pays for a rental car while your own car is being repaired after a covered claim.
INS-02.Gap insurance: Pays the difference when a car is totaled or stolen and you owe more on the loan or lease than the car is worth.
INS-02.Glass coverage: Pays to repair or replace a windshield or other window glass, often with a low deductible or none.
INS-02.New car replacement: Pays for a brand-new car of the same make and model if yours is totaled while still nearly new, instead of its depreciated value.
INS-02.Rideshare coverage: Fills the gaps in protection for people who drive for services such as Uber or Lyft, since personal policies often exclude that use.
INS-02.Mechanical breakdown insurance: Pays for repairs to major parts such as the engine or transmission that fail on their own, not because of an accident.
INS-02.Custom equipment coverage: Pays for parts added after the car left the factory, such as custom wheels or a stereo system, which standard coverage may limit.

INS-03.General liability: Covers claims that the business injured someone or damaged their property, such as a customer slipping in a store.
INS-03.Property insurance: Covers the firm's buildings, equipment and inventory against losses such as fire, theft and storm damage.
INS-03.Workers compensation: Pays medical costs and lost wages for employees hurt or made ill by their work. Most states require employers to carry it.
INS-03.Group health insurance: A health plan an employer buys to cover its employees, usually sharing the premium cost with them.
INS-03.Commercial auto: Covers vehicles the business owns or uses for work, including accidents its drivers cause.
INS-03.Product liability: Covers claims that a product the business made or sold injured someone or damaged property.
INS-03.Professional liability: Covers claims that a mistake or poor advice in a professional service cost a client money. Also called errors and omissions insurance.
INS-03.Business interruption: Replaces lost income and pays ongoing bills when a covered event, such as a fire, forces the business to close for a while.
INS-03.Cyber liability: Covers the costs of a data breach or computer attack, such as notifying customers, restoring systems and legal claims.
INS-03.Business owners policy: A package for small businesses that bundles property, general liability and business interruption coverage at a lower price.
INS-03.Key person insurance: Life or disability insurance a company buys on someone it depends on. The company receives the money if that person dies or cannot work.
INS-03.Directors and officers: Protects a company's leaders from personal loss if they are sued over decisions they made while running the company.
INS-03.Commercial umbrella: Extra liability coverage that pays once the limits of the firm's other liability policies are used up.
INS-03.Group life insurance: Life insurance an employer provides to its employees as a benefit, under one policy covering the whole group.
INS-03.Disability insurance: Coverage an employer offers that replaces part of an employee's pay if illness or injury keeps them from working.
INS-03.Flood or earthquake insurance: Separate policies for flood and earthquake damage, which standard commercial property insurance normally excludes.
INS-03.Employment practices liability: Covers claims by workers that the employer treated them unlawfully, such as discrimination, harassment or wrongful firing.
INS-03.Fidelity bond: Protects a business from losses caused by dishonest employees, such as theft of money or goods.
INS-03.Inland marine: Covers goods, tools and equipment while they are moved over land or kept away from the firm's main premises.
INS-03.Surety bond: A guarantee from a third party that the business will fulfill a contract or duty. If it fails, the bond pays the party that was let down.
INS-03.Equipment breakdown insurance: Pays to repair or replace machinery, such as boilers and cooling systems, that fails from mechanical or electrical causes.
INS-03.Liquor liability: Covers businesses that sell or serve alcohol against claims for harm caused by a customer who was served.
INS-03.Cargo insurance: Covers goods against loss or damage while they are being shipped by sea, air or land.
INS-03.Product recall insurance: Covers the cost of pulling a faulty or unsafe product from the market, such as notifying customers and collecting the goods.
INS-03.Pollution liability: Covers cleanup costs and claims when a business's operations contaminate land, water or air.
INS-03.Trade credit insurance: Pays the business if customers who bought on credit fail to pay their invoices, for example because they go bankrupt.

INS-04.Driving record: Your history of accidents and traffic tickets. A clean record signals lower risk and earns a lower price.
INS-04.Age: Young and newly licensed drivers have more crashes on average, so they are usually charged more.
INS-04.Type of car: The make, model, age and value of the vehicle. Cars that cost more to repair or are stolen more often cost more to insure.
INS-04.Location: Where you live and keep the car. Areas with more traffic, accidents, theft or severe weather have higher prices.
INS-04.Gender: Insurers in many states price men and women differently because their claim patterns differ on average. Some states ban this.
INS-04.Miles driven: How far you drive in a year. More time on the road means more chances of an accident.
INS-04.Credit history: Many insurers use a score based on your credit record because it tends to predict claims. Some states limit or ban the practice.
INS-04.Deductible: The amount you agree to pay toward a claim yourself. Choosing a higher one lowers the premium.
INS-04.Coverage amount: The types of coverage you pick and how high the limits are. More protection costs more.
INS-04.Claims history: How many insurance claims you have made before. Past claims suggest future ones are more likely.
INS-04.Marital status: Married drivers file fewer claims on average, so many insurers charge them slightly less.
INS-04.Driving experience: How many years you have held a license. More experience usually means a lower price.
INS-04.Good student status: Many insurers give a discount to students who keep good grades, treating it as a sign of responsibility.
INS-04.Safety features: Equipment such as airbags, automatic braking and anti-theft systems that makes injuries or theft less likely.
INS-04.Discounts and bundling: Price cuts for things such as insuring more than one car or buying home and auto policies from the same company.
INS-04.Driving habits: How you actually drive, such as speed and hard braking, measured by an app or device in programs you choose to join.
INS-04.Vehicle use: What the car is used for. Daily commuting or business driving usually costs more to insure than occasional personal trips.
INS-04.Continuous coverage: Whether you have stayed insured without a break. A gap in coverage often leads to a higher price.
INS-04.Occupation: Your job. Some insurers have found that claim rates differ by profession and adjust the price to match.
INS-04.Education level: The highest level of schooling completed, which some insurers use as a pricing factor where the state allows it.
INS-04.Homeownership: Whether you own your home. Some insurers charge homeowners less, treating it as a sign of financial stability.
INS-04.Where the car is parked: A car kept in a locked garage is less likely to be stolen or damaged than one left on the street.
INS-04.Driver training course: Completing an approved driver education or defensive driving class can earn a discount.

CRD-01.Credit card: Revolving credit that lets you borrow up to a limit again and again. Interest applies to any balance you do not pay off each month.
CRD-01.Mortgage: A long-term loan for buying a home, usually repaid monthly over 15 to 30 years. The home secures the loan.
CRD-01.Auto loan: A loan for buying a vehicle, repaid in monthly installments. The lender can repossess the vehicle if you stop paying.
CRD-01.Student loan: Money borrowed to pay for college or other education, from the government or a private lender, usually repaid after leaving school.
CRD-01.Personal loan: A fixed sum borrowed for almost any purpose and repaid in installments. It usually needs no collateral, so approval depends on your credit.
CRD-01.Payday loan: A small, very short-term loan due on your next payday. Its fees can amount to an extremely high yearly rate.
CRD-01.Small business loan: Money lent to a business to start up, buy equipment or cover running costs.
CRD-01.Home equity loan: A loan secured by the owner's equity, meaning the home's value minus what is still owed on the mortgage. It may be a lump sum or a line of credit.
CRD-01.Line of credit: An approved amount you can draw from as needed, repay and borrow again. Interest is charged only on what you use.
CRD-01.Buy now pay later: A plan offered at checkout that splits a purchase into a few installments, often with no interest if every payment is on time.
CRD-01.Store credit card: A credit card issued for one retailer, usable mainly in its stores. It often carries a higher interest rate than a general card.
CRD-01.Installment loan: A loan of a fixed amount repaid in equal scheduled payments over a set time, such as a car loan.
CRD-01.Secured or unsecured loan: A secured loan is backed by collateral the lender can take if you do not pay. An unsecured loan is backed only by your promise to repay.
CRD-01.Title loan: A short-term, high-cost loan that uses your car's title as collateral. The lender can take the car if you do not repay.
CRD-01.Pawn loan: A small loan from a pawnshop in exchange for leaving a valuable item. If you do not repay, the shop keeps and sells the item.
CRD-01.Debt consolidation loan: One new loan used to pay off several existing debts, leaving a single monthly payment, ideally at a lower interest rate.
CRD-01.Peer-to-peer loan: A loan arranged through an online platform that matches borrowers with individual investors instead of a bank.
CRD-01.Home improvement loan: A loan taken out to pay for repairs or renovations to a home.
CRD-01.Boat or RV loan: An installment loan for buying a boat, recreational vehicle or similar item. The item bought serves as collateral.
CRD-01.Cash advance: Cash borrowed against a credit card's limit. It usually carries a fee and a higher interest rate that starts right away.
CRD-01.Charge card: A card whose balance must be paid in full every month. Unlike a credit card, it does not let you carry debt forward.
CRD-01.Construction loan: A short-term loan that pays for building a home or other structure, with money released in stages as the work is done.
CRD-01.Bridge loan: A short-term loan that covers a gap until longer-term money arrives, such as buying a new home before the old one sells.
CRD-01.Margin loan: Money borrowed from a brokerage to buy investments, with the investments in the account serving as collateral.
CRD-01.401(k) loan: Money borrowed from your own workplace retirement account. You repay it, with interest, back into your account through payroll.
CRD-01.Credit-builder loan: A small loan where the lender holds the money in an account while you make payments. Its purpose is to build a good payment record.
CRD-01.Microloan: A very small loan, often to a new or tiny business that cannot get regular bank credit.

CRD-03.Payment history: A month-by-month record for each account showing whether you paid on time, paid late or missed payments.
CRD-03.Credit accounts: The list of your credit cards and loans, open and closed. The industry calls each one a tradeline.
CRD-03.Name: Your full name and any other names you have used, which the credit bureau uses to identify you.
CRD-03.Address: Your current home address and earlier ones, as reported by your lenders.
CRD-03.Social Security number: The government-issued number used to match credit records to the right person. Reports usually show only part of it.
CRD-03.Balances: How much you currently owe on each credit card and loan.
CRD-03.Credit limits: The most you are allowed to borrow on each credit card, or the original amount of each loan.
CRD-03.Hard inquiries: A record of each time a lender checked your report because you applied for credit. They stay listed for about two years.
CRD-03.Bankruptcies: Court filings in which a person asked for legal relief from debts they could not pay. They stay on a report for years.
CRD-03.Date of birth: Your birth date, used along with your name and Social Security number to confirm your identity.
CRD-03.Account status: Whether each account is open, closed, paid off, current or behind on payments.
CRD-03.Creditor names: The names of the banks, card issuers and other lenders that hold each of your accounts.
CRD-03.Collections: Unpaid debts that the original lender has handed or sold to a collection agency. They seriously hurt your credit.
CRD-03.Employer: Current or past employers you listed on credit applications. The report uses this to identify you and does not show your pay.
CRD-03.Account opening dates: The date each account was opened, which shows how long you have been using credit.
CRD-03.Phone number: Contact numbers you have given to lenders, kept as part of your identifying details.
CRD-03.Account types: The kind of credit each account is, such as a revolving credit card, an installment loan or a mortgage.
CRD-03.Foreclosures: Records of a lender taking back a home because the mortgage was not paid.
CRD-03.Charge-offs: Debts a lender has given up expecting to collect and written off as a loss. You still owe the money.
CRD-03.Repossessions: Records of a lender taking back property, usually a car, because the loan on it was not paid.
CRD-03.Soft inquiries: Checks of your report that are not tied to a credit application, such as your own check. Only you see them and they do not affect your score.
CRD-03.Fraud alert or security freeze: Notes you can add to protect against identity theft. An alert tells lenders to verify your identity, and a freeze blocks new credit checks.

CRD-04.Interest rate: The percentage charged on the amount you owe. The agreement says whether it is fixed or can change over time.
CRD-04.APR: Annual percentage rate. The yearly cost of borrowing shown as a percentage, including interest and certain fees, so offers can be compared.
CRD-04.Principal: The amount of money actually borrowed, before any interest or fees are added.
CRD-04.Fees: Charges on top of interest that the lender may collect, each of which must be listed in the agreement.
CRD-04.Required payment: How much you must pay and when, such as a fixed monthly loan payment or a credit card's minimum payment and due date.
CRD-04.Term: The length of time you have to repay the loan, such as 60 months for a car loan.
CRD-04.Late fee: A charge added when your payment arrives after the due date.
CRD-04.Credit limit: The maximum balance you are allowed to carry on a credit card or line of credit.
CRD-04.Collateral: Property you pledge to back the loan, such as a car or house, which the lender can take if you do not repay.
CRD-04.Grace period: The time between the end of a card's billing cycle and the due date. Pay in full within it and no interest is charged on purchases.
CRD-04.Annual fee: A yearly charge some credit cards make simply for having the card.
CRD-04.Default: Failing to meet the agreement, usually by missing payments. The contract spells out what the lender can do when this happens.
CRD-04.Down payment: The part of the purchase price you pay up front in cash. The loan covers the rest.
CRD-04.Finance charge: The total dollar cost of the credit, including interest and certain fees.
CRD-04.Amortization: The schedule showing how each payment is split between interest and principal as the loan is gradually paid down.
CRD-04.Prepayment penalty: A fee some lenders charge if you pay off the loan earlier than scheduled.
CRD-04.Origination fee: An upfront fee for processing and setting up a new loan, often a percentage of the amount borrowed.
CRD-04.Penalty APR: A much higher interest rate a card issuer can apply after a serious violation, such as paying very late.
CRD-04.Introductory rate: A low starting interest rate, sometimes zero, that lasts for a limited time before the regular rate begins.
CRD-04.Cosigner: A second person who signs the loan and promises to repay it if the main borrower does not.
CRD-04.Total of payments: The full amount you will have paid by the end of the loan, counting principal, interest and fees, if every payment is made as scheduled.
CRD-04.Balloon payment: One large payment due at the end of a loan whose earlier payments were too small to pay off the full balance.
CRD-04.Acceleration clause: A term that lets the lender demand the entire remaining balance at once if the borrower defaults.
CRD-04.Balance transfer fee: A fee, usually a percentage of the amount moved, for shifting debt from one credit card to another.
CRD-04.Cash advance fee: A fee for using a credit card to withdraw cash, charged in addition to the interest on the amount taken.
CRD-04.Foreign transaction fee: A percentage a card issuer adds to purchases made abroad or in another currency.
CRD-04.Over-limit fee: A fee for letting your balance go above the credit limit. Card issuers may charge it only if you agreed to allow such transactions.
CRD-04.Arbitration clause: A term requiring disputes to be settled by a private arbitrator instead of in court, often ruling out group lawsuits.
CRD-04.Balance calculation method: The rule for working out the balance interest is charged on. Most cards use the average daily balance over the billing cycle.

CRD-05.Bankruptcy: A court process for people who cannot pay their debts. Some debts are wiped out or put on a repayment plan, at serious cost to credit.
CRD-05.Debt consolidation: Combining several debts into one new loan with a single payment, ideally at a lower interest rate.
CRD-05.Refinancing: Replacing an existing loan with a new one on better terms, such as a lower interest rate or smaller monthly payment.
CRD-05.Negotiating with the lender: Contacting the lender to explain the hardship and ask for easier terms, such as a payment plan. Lenders often prefer this to a default.
CRD-05.Credit counseling: Advice from a trained counselor, often at a nonprofit agency, who reviews your budget and debts and helps you plan how to repay.
CRD-05.Debt settlement: An agreement in which the creditor accepts less than the full amount owed as payment in full. It usually damages your credit.
CRD-05.Deferment: A lender-approved pause in payments for a set time. On some federal student loans, interest does not build up during the pause.
CRD-05.Forbearance: A temporary pause or reduction in payments granted during hardship. Interest usually keeps building and must be paid later.
CRD-05.Balance transfer: Moving credit card debt to another card with a lower rate, often a temporary zero percent offer, so more of each payment cuts the balance.
CRD-05.Lower interest rate: A reduction in the rate charged on the debt, which some lenders grant on request. It lowers the cost of repaying.
CRD-05.Loan modification: A permanent change to the terms of an existing loan, often a mortgage, such as a lower rate or longer term, to make payments affordable.
CRD-05.Debt management plan: A program run by a credit counseling agency. You make one monthly payment to the agency, which pays creditors, often at reduced rates.
CRD-05.Income-driven repayment: Federal student loan plans that set the monthly payment as a share of the borrower's income instead of the amount owed.
CRD-05.Loan forgiveness: Cancellation of all or part of a debt so it no longer has to be repaid, as in some federal student loan programs for public service.
CRD-05.Extended repayment plan: Stretching the loan over a longer time to shrink each payment. The trade-off is paying more interest in total.
CRD-05.Short sale: Selling a home for less than the mortgage balance, with the lender's agreement, to avoid foreclosure.
CRD-05.Deed in lieu of foreclosure: Voluntarily handing ownership of a home to the lender to settle the mortgage and avoid the foreclosure process.
CRD-05.Voluntary surrender: Giving the collateral, usually a car, back to the lender yourself instead of waiting for it to be repossessed. You may still owe a balance.
CRD-05.Loan rehabilitation: A program for defaulted federal student loans. Making a set series of agreed on-time payments takes the loan out of default.

BNK-05.Signature: The account holder's signed name at the bottom right. It authorizes the bank to pay the check.
BNK-05.Amount: How much is to be paid, written twice: once in numbers in the box and once in words on the line below the payee.
BNK-05.Date: The day the check is written, placed at the top right.
BNK-05.Payee: The person or business being paid, written on the line that begins "Pay to the order of".
BNK-05.Memo: An optional line at the bottom left for noting what the payment is for, such as a bill's account number.
BNK-05.Account number: The number that identifies the writer's own checking account at the bank. It is printed along the bottom edge.
BNK-05.Routing number: A nine-digit number printed at the bottom left that identifies the bank the check is drawn on.
BNK-05.Check number: The number that identifies this particular check, printed at the top right and again along the bottom, for record keeping.
BNK-05.Account holder name and address: The details of the person who owns the account, printed at the top left.
BNK-05.Bank name: The name of the bank that holds the account and will pay the check, printed on its face.
BNK-05.Endorsement: The payee's signature on the back of the check, needed to cash or deposit it.
BNK-05.MICR line: The row of numbers along the bottom printed in magnetic ink so machines can read the routing, account and check numbers. MICR is magnetic ink character recognition.
BNK-05.Fractional number: A small fraction-style number near the top right that also identifies the bank. It is a backup in case the bottom line cannot be read.

BNK-06.Medium of exchange: A function of money: people accept it in payment for goods and services, so there is no need to barter.
BNK-06.Store of value: A function of money: it holds its buying power over time, so you can save it today and spend it later.
BNK-06.Durability: Money must survive being handled and passed around many times without wearing out quickly.
BNK-06.Portability: Money must be easy to carry and move, so people can take it wherever they trade.
BNK-06.Unit of account: A function of money: it gives a common measure for stating prices, so the values of different things can be compared.
BNK-06.Divisibility: Money must break down into smaller units, so people can pay exact amounts and make change.
BNK-06.Acceptability: Money works only if nearly everyone in the economy is willing to take it as payment.
BNK-06.Limited supply: Money must be scarce enough to keep its value. If there were too much of it, each unit would buy less.
BNK-06.Uniformity: Every unit of the same denomination must be identical and worth the same, so one dollar is as good as any other.
BNK-06.Stability of value: Money's buying power should stay fairly steady, so people can trust it for saving and long-term deals.
BNK-06.Recognizability: People must be able to tell easily that money is genuine and what it is worth.
BNK-06.Standard of deferred payment: A function of money: debts can be stated in it today and settled in it at a future date.
BNK-06.Difficult to counterfeit: Money must be hard to fake. Otherwise copies would flood in and destroy trust in it and its value.

BNK-07.Conduct monetary policy: Influence interest rates and the supply of money and credit in order to steer the economy toward its goals.
BNK-07.Supervise and regulate banks: Set rules for banks and inspect them to make sure they are run safely and treat customers lawfully.
BNK-07.Keep prices stable: One of the two main goals Congress gave the Fed: keep inflation low and steady so money holds its buying power.
BNK-07.Promote maximum employment: One of the two main goals Congress gave the Fed: support conditions in which as many people as possible who want jobs can find them.
BNK-07.Maintain financial stability: Watch for and reduce risks that could cause the whole financial system to break down, as in a banking panic.
BNK-07.Distribute currency: Put paper money and coins into circulation by supplying them to banks, and remove worn-out notes.
BNK-07.Lender of last resort: Lend to sound banks that cannot get funds elsewhere in an emergency, so a cash shortage does not turn into a panic.
BNK-07.Operate the payments system: Run the networks that move money between banks, such as check clearing, wire transfers and electronic payments.
BNK-07.Promote economic growth: A broad aim behind the Fed's formal goals: a healthy, steadily growing economy without sharp booms and busts.
BNK-07.Serve as the bank for the federal govern: Hold the U.S. Treasury's accounts, process the government's payments and help it sell its bonds.
BNK-07.Hold bank reserves: Act as a bank for banks. Commercial banks keep deposits, called reserves, in accounts at the Fed.
BNK-07.Protect consumers: Help write and enforce rules that make sure banks treat customers fairly in lending and other services.
BNK-07.Set reserve requirements: Decide what share of customer deposits banks must keep in reserve instead of lending out.
BNK-07.Moderate long-term interest rates: A third goal named in the law that guides the Fed. It tends to follow naturally when prices are kept stable.
BNK-07.Economic research: Collect data and study the economy to guide its decisions, publishing reports such as the Beige Book on regional conditions.
BNK-07.Promote community development: Support access to credit and financial services in lower-income communities through research, outreach and bank oversight.

INS-05.Fire: Flames that damage or destroy the house and its contents. Fire is the classic peril every standard policy covers.
INS-05.Theft: Belongings stolen from the home, along with damage done by someone breaking in.
INS-05.Windstorm: Damage from strong winds, including tornadoes, such as a roof torn off. Some coastal areas need separate wind coverage.
INS-05.Hail: Damage from balls of ice falling in a storm, which commonly dent or break roofs, siding and windows.
INS-05.Lightning: Damage from a lightning strike, including any fire it starts and harm to wiring and electronics.
INS-05.Vandalism: Deliberate damage to the property by someone else, such as broken windows or spray paint.
INS-05.Burst pipes: Sudden, accidental water damage from plumbing that bursts or freezes. A slow leak left unrepaired is not covered.
INS-05.Smoke: Sudden, accidental smoke damage to walls, furniture and belongings, even if the fire itself was small or nearby.
INS-05.Falling objects: Damage from something landing on the house, most often a tree or large branch.
INS-05.Explosion: Damage from a blast, such as one caused by a gas leak or a faulty appliance.
INS-05.Weight of ice or snow: Damage, such as a collapsed roof, caused by heavy snow, ice or sleet building up on the structure.
INS-05.Damage from vehicles: Harm to the home when a car or truck crashes into it.
INS-05.Riot or civil commotion: Damage to the property during a riot or other violent public disturbance.
INS-05.Injury to a guest: Not property damage but the policy's liability side: it pays if a visitor is hurt on your property and you are responsible.
INS-05.Damage from aircraft: Harm caused by an aircraft, or parts falling from one, striking the property.
INS-05.Volcanic eruption: Damage from a volcano's blast, lava flow or ash. Earthquakes and tremors linked to it are generally excluded.
INS-05.Power surge: Sudden, accidental damage to wiring, appliances or electronics from a spike in electrical current.
INS-05.Water heater or heating system rupture: Sudden, accidental cracking, bursting or tearing apart of a water heater, boiler or similar household system.

INS-06.Term life: Covers a set number of years, such as 20. It pays only if the insured dies during that time and builds no savings, so it costs least.
INS-06.Whole life: Permanent coverage that lasts for life, with a fixed premium and a savings part, called cash value, that grows at a guaranteed rate.
INS-06.Permanent life: The general name for policies that last for the insured's whole life and build cash value, such as whole life and universal life.
INS-06.Universal life: Permanent coverage with flexibility. The owner can adjust premium payments and the death benefit within limits, and cash value earns interest.
INS-06.Group life: Coverage provided to a group of people under one policy, most often by an employer as a job benefit.
INS-06.Variable life: Permanent coverage whose cash value is invested in funds the owner chooses, so it can rise or fall with the markets.
INS-06.Final expense: A small permanent policy meant to pay funeral costs and other bills left at death.
INS-06.Variable universal life: Permanent coverage that combines the flexible premiums of universal life with the investment choices of variable life.
INS-06.Indexed universal life: Universal life whose cash value growth is linked to a stock market index, usually with a floor against losses and a cap on gains.
INS-06.Credit life: A policy that pays off a specific debt, such as a loan or mortgage, if the borrower dies. The payout goes to the lender.
INS-06.Decreasing term: Term insurance whose payout shrinks over the years, often arranged to match a mortgage balance that is being paid down.
INS-06.Renewable term: Term insurance that can be renewed at the end of each term without a new medical exam, though the premium rises with age.
INS-06.Survivorship life: One policy covering two people, usually spouses, that pays out only after the second person dies.
INS-06.Endowment: A policy that pays the face amount if the insured dies during the term, or pays it to the insured if they are still alive at the end.
INS-06.Guaranteed issue life: A policy with no health questions or medical exam, so nobody in the eligible age range is turned down. It costs more for limited coverage.
INS-06.Simplified issue life: A policy that needs no medical exam, only answers to some health questions. It is quicker to get but costs more.
INS-06.Convertible term: Term insurance that can be switched to a permanent policy later without having to prove good health.
INS-06.Return of premium term: Term insurance that refunds the premiums paid if the insured outlives the term. It costs more than ordinary term.
INS-06.Limited pay life: Whole life insurance where premiums are paid for only a set number of years or to a set age, but coverage lasts for life.
INS-06.Single premium life: Permanent coverage paid for with one large payment up front instead of ongoing premiums.
INS-06.Joint life: One policy covering two people that pays out when the first of them dies, after which the coverage ends.

CRD-06.Down payment: The part of the home's price the buyer pays in cash at closing. The mortgage covers the rest.
CRD-06.Closing costs: The overall name for the fees and prepaid items due when the sale is finalized, on top of the down payment.
CRD-06.Home inspection: A fee for a professional to examine the house for defects, such as roof or plumbing problems, before the buyer commits.
CRD-06.Appraisal fee: A fee for a licensed appraiser to estimate the home's market value, so the lender knows the house is worth the loan.
CRD-06.Homeowners insurance: Lenders require proof the home is insured, so the buyer usually pays the first year's premium at or before closing.
CRD-06.Property taxes: The buyer's share of the local tax on the home, often paid in advance at closing for the months ahead.
CRD-06.Private mortgage insurance: Insurance that protects the lender if the buyer stops paying. It is usually required on conventional loans with a small down payment.
CRD-06.Origination fee: The lender's charge for processing, underwriting and setting up the mortgage.
CRD-06.Title search and insurance: A check of public records to confirm the seller truly owns the home, plus insurance in case an ownership problem surfaces later.
CRD-06.Attorney fees: Payment to a lawyer who reviews the documents and may run the closing. Some states require one.
CRD-06.Earnest money: A deposit made with the offer to show the buyer is serious. It is held by a neutral party and credited toward the purchase at closing.
CRD-06.Discount points: Optional fees paid to the lender up front in exchange for a lower interest rate. One point equals 1 percent of the loan amount.
CRD-06.Prepaid interest: Interest on the mortgage for the days between closing and the end of that month, collected at closing.
CRD-06.Application fee: A charge some lenders make for taking and starting to process the mortgage application.
CRD-06.Credit report fee: The cost of the lender pulling the buyer's credit reports and scores to judge the application.
CRD-06.Settlement fee: The charge by the title or escrow company that runs the closing, handles the paperwork and pays out the money.
CRD-06.Recording fees: Charges by the local government for entering the new deed and mortgage in the public records.
CRD-06.Survey fee: The cost of a surveyor confirming the property's boundary lines and the location of structures on it.
CRD-06.Escrow deposit: Money collected at closing to start an account from which the lender will pay future property tax and insurance bills.
CRD-06.Transfer tax: A tax some states and localities charge when ownership of real estate changes hands. Who pays it varies by place.
CRD-06.Pest inspection: A fee for checking the house for termites and other wood-destroying insects. Some lenders and loan programs require it.
CRD-06.Flood certification fee: A small charge for a report stating whether the home lies in a flood zone, which determines if flood insurance is required.
CRD-06.VA funding fee: A one-time charge on most home loans backed by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), which helps fund the program.
CRD-06.Rate lock fee: A charge some lenders make for guaranteeing the quoted interest rate for a set time while the loan is processed.
CRD-06.HOA fees: Dues and transfer charges owed to a homeowners association (HOA), the group that runs a community's shared areas and rules.

CRD-07.Fixed-rate mortgage: A home loan whose interest rate never changes, so the principal and interest payment is the same every month for the whole loan.
CRD-07.Adjustable-rate mortgage: A home loan whose interest rate is fixed for an opening period and then moves up or down with a market benchmark.
CRD-07.FHA loan: A mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration. It allows smaller down payments and lower credit scores than most other loans.
CRD-07.VA loan: A mortgage backed by the Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible service members and veterans, often with no down payment.
CRD-07.Conventional loan: A mortgage from a private lender that is not insured or guaranteed by a government agency.
CRD-07.Jumbo loan: A mortgage larger than the limit that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will buy. It usually has stricter credit requirements.
CRD-07.Second mortgage: An additional loan secured by a home that already has a mortgage, such as a home equity loan. It is repaid after the first if the home is sold.
CRD-07.Government-backed loan: A mortgage that a federal agency insures or guarantees, so the lender is protected if the borrower defaults. FHA, VA and USDA loans are examples.
CRD-07.Reverse mortgage: A loan that lets older homeowners draw on their home equity without monthly payments. It is repaid when they sell, move out or die.
CRD-07.USDA loan: A mortgage backed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture for low- and moderate-income buyers in eligible rural areas, often with no down payment.
CRD-07.Interest-only mortgage: A home loan where early payments cover only interest. The balance does not shrink until later, when payments jump.
CRD-07.Subprime mortgage: A home loan made to a borrower with weak credit. It carries a higher interest rate to make up for the greater risk of default.
CRD-07.Refinance loan: A new mortgage that pays off and replaces an existing one, usually to get a lower rate, change the term or take out cash.
CRD-07.Balloon mortgage: A home loan with low payments for a few years, followed by one very large payment of the remaining balance.
CRD-07.Construction loan: A short-term loan that pays for building a house, with money released in stages. It is often converted to a regular mortgage after.
CRD-07.Conforming loan: A mortgage that meets the size limit and other standards set for purchase by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
CRD-07.Bridge loan: A short-term loan that lets a buyer purchase a new home before the sale of the current one is complete.
CRD-07.Graduated payment mortgage: A home loan whose payments start low and rise on a set schedule over the first years, suited to buyers who expect rising income.
CRD-07.Assumable mortgage: A home loan that a buyer can take over from the seller, keeping the existing interest rate and remaining balance.
CRD-07.Seller financing: An arrangement where the seller acts as the lender. The buyer makes payments directly to the seller instead of to a bank.
CRD-07.Renovation loan: A mortgage that covers both the price of a home and the cost of repairing or improving it, in a single loan.
CRD-07.Wraparound mortgage: A form of seller financing in which the seller keeps the existing mortgage and gives the buyer a new, larger loan that includes it.

INV-06.401(k): A retirement plan offered by an employer. Workers put in part of each paycheck before income tax, and many employers add matching money.
INV-06.Roth IRA: An individual retirement account funded with money that has already been taxed. Qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
INV-06.Traditional IRA: An individual retirement account a person opens on their own. Contributions may be tax-deductible, and withdrawals in retirement are taxed.
INV-06.Pension plan: An employer-funded plan that promises a regular income in retirement, usually based on salary and years of service.
INV-06.529 plan: A state-sponsored account for education savings. The money grows tax-free and comes out tax-free when spent on qualified school costs.
INV-06.Health savings account: An account for medical costs, open to people with a high-deductible health plan. Money goes in, grows and comes out for medical bills tax-free.
INV-06.403(b): A retirement plan much like a 401(k), offered to employees of public schools, hospitals and other nonprofit organizations.
INV-06.Roth 401(k): A workplace retirement plan option funded with after-tax pay. Qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
INV-06.Flexible spending account: An employer account where workers set aside pre-tax pay for medical or dependent care costs. Most of it must be used within the plan year.
INV-06.SEP IRA: A Simplified Employee Pension. A retirement account for self-employed people and small businesses, funded by the employer's contributions.
INV-06.SIMPLE IRA: The Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees. A retirement plan for small businesses, with worker contributions and required employer contributions.
INV-06.457 plan: A retirement savings plan for state and local government workers and some nonprofit employees, funded from pre-tax pay.
INV-06.Annuity: An insurance contract in which money grows tax-deferred and is later paid out as income, often for the rest of the owner's life.
INV-06.Rollover IRA: An individual retirement account used to receive money moved out of a former employer's plan, keeping its tax advantages.
INV-06.Defined contribution plan: Any retirement plan where set amounts go into a worker's own account and the final benefit depends on how the investments perform.
INV-06.Thrift Savings Plan: The retirement savings plan for federal employees and members of the military, similar to a 401(k).
INV-06.Coverdell education savings account: An account for a child's education costs, including school before college. Earnings are tax-free when spent on qualified expenses.
INV-06.Solo 401(k): A 401(k) for a self-employed person with no employees other than a spouse. The owner contributes as both employer and employee.
INV-06.ABLE account: A tax-advantaged savings account for people with disabilities. It lets them save without losing eligibility for certain public benefits.
INV-06.Profit-sharing plan: A retirement plan in which the employer decides each year how much of its profits to put into employees' accounts.
INV-06.Employee stock ownership plan: A retirement plan that invests mainly in the employer's own stock, giving workers an ownership stake in the company.
INV-06.Keogh plan: An older name for tax-deferred retirement plans set up by self-employed people and unincorporated businesses.
INV-06.Health reimbursement arrangement: An employer-funded arrangement that repays workers, tax-free, for qualified medical costs. Only the employer puts money in.
INV-06.Spousal IRA: An individual retirement account that a working spouse funds on behalf of a husband or wife with little or no income.
INV-06.Money purchase plan: A retirement plan in which the employer must contribute a fixed percentage of each worker's pay every year.
INV-06.SIMPLE 401(k): A simplified 401(k) for small businesses. Workers can contribute and the employer must make contributions, which belong to the workers at once.

INV-07.Technology: Companies that make software, computer hardware and semiconductor chips, or provide information technology services.
INV-07.Health care: Drug makers, biotechnology firms, medical device makers, hospitals and health insurers.
INV-07.Energy: Companies that find, produce, refine and transport oil, natural gas and coal, along with the firms that supply them with equipment.
INV-07.Financials: Banks, insurance companies, brokerages and other firms whose business is handling money.
INV-07.Real estate: Companies that own, develop or manage property, including real estate investment trusts (REITs).
INV-07.Utilities: Companies that supply electricity, natural gas and water. Demand is steady, so their profits and dividends tend to be stable.
INV-07.Industrials: Makers of machinery, aircraft and building products, along with transport firms such as airlines and railroads.
INV-07.Consumer discretionary: Companies selling things people want but can put off buying, such as cars, restaurant meals and travel. Sales fall in hard times.
INV-07.Consumer staples: Companies selling everyday necessities such as food, drinks and household goods. Sales hold up even in a downturn.
INV-07.Communication services: Phone and internet providers, together with media, entertainment and social media companies.
INV-07.Materials: Companies that produce raw materials such as chemicals, metals, paper and packaging for other industries to use.

FIN-07.Stock market: Where shares of ownership in public companies are bought and sold.
FIN-07.Bond market: Where governments and companies borrow by selling bonds, and where investors trade those bonds.
FIN-07.Foreign exchange market: Where one country's currency is traded for another's. It is the largest financial market in the world by daily trading.
FIN-07.Commodities market: Where raw materials such as oil, gold and wheat are traded, often through contracts for future delivery.
FIN-07.Cryptocurrency market: Where digital currencies such as Bitcoin are traded, mostly on online platforms that run around the clock.
FIN-07.Money market: Where very short-term loans and debt, maturing in a year or less, are traded. Treasury bills and commercial paper are examples.
FIN-07.Capital market: Where long-term funds are raised and traded. It is the combined name for the stock and bond markets.
FIN-07.Derivatives market: Where contracts such as futures and options are traded. Their value comes from the price of something else, such as a stock or commodity.
FIN-07.Primary market: Where new stocks and bonds are sold for the first time and the money goes to the issuer, as in an initial public offering.
FIN-07.Secondary market: Where investors trade existing securities with each other. The company that issued them receives none of the money.
FIN-07.Mortgage market: Where home loans are made and then sold on to investors, often bundled together into mortgage-backed securities.
FIN-07.Over-the-counter market: Trading done directly between dealers over electronic networks instead of on a central exchange.
FIN-07.Spot market: Where an asset is bought and sold for immediate payment and delivery at the current price.
FIN-07.Auction market: A market where buyers post bids and sellers post asking prices at the same time, and trades occur where the two match.
FIN-07.Interbank market: Where banks lend to each other, often overnight, and trade currencies among themselves.
FIN-07.Third or fourth market: The third market is off-exchange dealer trading of exchange-listed stocks. The fourth is direct trading between big institutions, with no broker.
FIN-07.Private equity market: Where investors buy stakes in companies that are not listed on a stock exchange, including venture capital for startups.

FIN-08.Operating budget: The plan for the revenue and expenses of day-to-day business over the coming period. It leads to a budgeted income statement.
FIN-08.Sales budget: The forecast of units to be sold and the revenue they will bring in. It is prepared first because the other budgets depend on it.
FIN-08.Cash budget: A plan of expected cash coming in and going out each period, showing when the business may run short or have extra.
FIN-08.Marketing budget: The amount set aside for advertising, promotion and other efforts to attract customers.
FIN-08.Start-up budget: An estimate of the one-time costs of opening a new business, such as equipment, licenses and opening inventory.
FIN-08.Capital budget: The plan for spending on long-lived assets such as buildings, machinery and vehicles.
FIN-08.Master budget: The complete set of a company's budgets for a period, combining the operating and financial budgets into one overall plan.
FIN-08.Production budget: The number of units that must be made to meet expected sales and leave the desired amount of inventory at period end.
FIN-08.Project budget: The planned costs of one specific project, such as launching a product or building a new store.
FIN-08.Departmental budget: The planned spending, and any revenue, for one department of the business, such as human resources.
FIN-08.Direct labor budget: The hours of production work needed to meet the production budget, and what that labor will cost.
FIN-08.Direct materials budget: The quantity and cost of raw materials that must be bought to meet the production plan.
FIN-08.Overhead budget: The expected factory costs other than direct materials and direct labor, such as factory rent, utilities and supervision.
FIN-08.Selling and administrative expense budge: The planned costs outside the factory, such as sales commissions, advertising and office salaries.
FIN-08.Financial budget: The part of the master budget covering cash and financing: the cash budget, capital budget and budgeted balance sheet.
FIN-08.Research and development budget: The amount set aside for creating new products and improving existing ones.
FIN-08.Flexible budget: A budget that adjusts its revenue and cost figures to the actual level of activity, making comparisons with results fairer.
FIN-08.Static budget: A budget built for one planned level of activity. Its figures do not change even if actual sales or output turn out different.
FIN-08.Zero-based budget: A budget built from zero each period. Every expense must be justified afresh instead of starting from last year's numbers.
FIN-08.Incremental budget: A budget made by taking last period's figures and adjusting them up or down by a small amount.
FIN-08.Rolling budget: A budget that is continually extended. As each month or quarter ends, a new one is added so the plan always covers a full period ahead.
FIN-08.Activity-based budget: A budget built from the cost of the activities needed to produce and sell, such as machine setups or deliveries.
FIN-08.Budgeted financial statements: A projected income statement and balance sheet showing what results will look like if the budget plans are met.
FIN-08.Ending inventory budget: The planned quantity and cost of unsold goods and materials on hand at the end of the period.
FIN-08.Cost of goods sold budget: The expected cost of the products to be sold, built from the materials, labor and overhead budgets and inventory levels.

PFL-08.Wages or salary: Pay for working at a job. Wages are paid by the hour, and a salary is a fixed amount for the year.
PFL-08.Investment income: Money earned from owning investments, such as interest, dividends and gains from selling at a profit.
PFL-08.Tips: Extra money customers give service workers, such as restaurant servers, on top of the bill. They count as taxable income.
PFL-08.Commission: Pay based on results, usually a percentage of the sales a worker makes.
PFL-08.Bonus: An extra payment from an employer on top of regular pay, often a reward for good performance or a good company year.
PFL-08.Interest: Money a bank or borrower pays you for the use of your money, such as on a savings account or a bond.
PFL-08.Dividends: A share of a company's profits paid out to people who own its stock.
PFL-08.Self-employment income: The profit a person earns from running their own business or doing freelance or gig work.
PFL-08.Rental income: Money received from tenants for the use of property you own, such as an apartment or house.
PFL-08.Government benefits: Payments from public programs, such as Social Security, unemployment benefits or disability payments.
PFL-08.Capital gains: The profit from selling an asset, such as stock or property, for more than you paid for it.
PFL-08.Pension: Regular payments in retirement from a former employer's plan, or withdrawals from retirement savings accounts.
PFL-08.Gifts or inheritance: Money or property received from family or others, either while they are living or after they die.
PFL-08.Child support or alimony: Court-ordered payments received from a former partner, either to help raise a child or to support a former spouse.
PFL-08.Selling personal items: Cash raised by selling things you own and no longer need, such as clothes, electronics or furniture.
PFL-08.Royalties: Payments for letting others use something you created or own, such as a song, a book or a patent.
PFL-08.Scholarships or grants: Money awarded for education or another purpose that does not have to be repaid.
PFL-08.Lottery or gambling winnings: Money won through games of chance. It is irregular and uncertain, and it is taxable.
PFL-08.Trust fund: Money or property held and managed for a person under a legal arrangement, with payments made to them according to its terms.
PFL-08.Annuity payments: Regular income paid under an annuity contract, usually by an insurance company, often for the rest of the owner's life.

ACC-08.Financial accounting: Prepares the financial statements that report a company's results to outsiders such as investors, lenders and regulators.
ACC-08.Tax accounting: Deals with preparing tax returns and planning ahead so a person or business pays no more tax than the law requires.
ACC-08.Managerial accounting: Produces reports and analysis for a company's own managers to use in planning, controlling costs and making decisions.
ACC-08.Auditing: The independent examination of financial records to judge whether they are accurate and follow the rules.
ACC-08.Cost accounting: Tracks and analyzes what it costs to make a product or deliver a service, to help set prices and control spending.
ACC-08.Public accounting: Firms that serve many outside clients, offering auditing, tax and advisory work, usually through certified public accountants.
ACC-08.Bookkeeping: The routine recording of daily transactions, such as sales, purchases and payments, in the accounting records.
ACC-08.Forensic accounting: Investigates financial records for fraud and other wrongdoing. The findings are often used as evidence in court.
ACC-08.Governmental accounting: Tracks how federal, state and local governments raise and spend public money, with a focus on accountability to taxpayers.
ACC-08.Private accounting: Working as an accountant inside a single company, handling only that employer's records and reports.
ACC-08.Nonprofit accounting: Serves charities and similar organizations. It focuses on showing that donations and grants were used for their intended purposes.
ACC-08.Payroll accounting: Calculates employees' pay, withholds the correct taxes and deductions, and keeps the records the law requires.
ACC-08.Budgeting: Prepares financial plans for future periods and compares actual results against them.
ACC-08.Consulting: Advice accountants give clients on improving operations, systems or financial strategy, beyond audit and tax work.
ACC-08.Accounting information systems: Designs and manages the software and procedures used to collect, store and report accounting data.
ACC-08.International accounting: Deals with business across borders, including foreign currencies and reporting rules used abroad, such as IFRS, the international standards.
ACC-08.Fiduciary accounting: Keeps the records for money and property managed on someone else's behalf, such as a trust or the estate of a person who has died.
ACC-08.Environmental accounting: Measures and reports the environmental costs of a business's activities, such as pollution, waste and cleanup.
ACC-08.Project accounting: Tracks the costs, revenue and progress of individual projects separately from the rest of the business.

INS-07.HMO: A health maintenance organization covers care only from doctors and hospitals in its network. You usually need a referral from your primary care doctor to see a specialist.
INS-07.PPO: A preferred provider organization charges less when you use its network but still pays part of the bill for outside providers. No referral is needed to see a specialist.
INS-07.Medicare: The federal health insurance program for people 65 and older and for some younger people with disabilities.
INS-07.Medicaid: A program run jointly by the federal government and the states that pays for health care for people with low incomes.
INS-07.Employer-sponsored plan: Group health coverage offered through a job. The employer usually pays part of the premium and the rest comes out of the worker's paycheck.
INS-07.High-deductible health plan: A plan with a lower premium but a higher deductible, so you pay more of your own bills before coverage starts. It can be paired with a health savings account.
INS-07.Marketplace plan: A private plan bought through the government-run exchange created by the Affordable Care Act. People who qualify get help paying the premium.
INS-07.CHIP: The Children's Health Insurance Program gives low-cost coverage to children in families that earn too much for Medicaid but cannot afford private insurance.
INS-07.COBRA: A federal law that lets workers keep their employer's group health plan for a limited time after leaving a job. They usually have to pay the full premium themselves.
INS-07.EPO: An exclusive provider organization covers only care inside its network, except in an emergency. Unlike most HMOs, it usually does not require a referral to see a specialist.
INS-07.POS plan: A point-of-service plan mixes the HMO and PPO designs. You pick a primary care doctor who gives referrals, but you may go outside the network at a higher cost.
INS-07.Medicare Advantage: Also called Medicare Part C. Private insurers approved by Medicare provide the hospital and medical coverage in one plan, often with drug coverage included.
INS-07.Catastrophic plan: A plan with a very low premium and a very high deductible, aimed mainly at young adults. It protects against the cost of a serious illness or accident.
INS-07.TRICARE: The health care program for U.S. military service members, military retirees and their families.
INS-07.Short-term health insurance: Temporary coverage meant to fill a gap, such as between jobs. It covers less than a regular plan and can turn down people with existing health problems.
INS-07.Bronze, silver, gold or platinum plan: The metal levels of Marketplace plans. Bronze has the lowest premiums but the highest costs when you get care, and platinum is the reverse.
INS-07.Medigap: Medicare supplement insurance sold by private companies. It pays some costs that Original Medicare leaves to the patient, such as deductibles and coinsurance.
INS-07.Medicare Part D: The part of Medicare that helps pay for prescription drugs. The coverage is provided through private plans approved by Medicare.
INS-07.Veterans health care: Health care provided by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs to eligible people who served in the military.
INS-07.Indian Health Service: A federal agency that provides health care to members of federally recognized American Indian and Alaska Native tribes.
INS-07.Fee-for-service plan: The traditional design, also called an indemnity plan. You can see almost any doctor, and the insurer pays a share of each bill after your deductible.
INS-07.Student health plan: Health coverage that a college or university offers to its enrolled students.
INS-07.Dental or vision plan: A separate plan that helps pay for dental care or for eye exams and glasses. Regular health plans for adults often leave these out, so they are sold on their own or as add-ons.

INS-08.Flood: Water that rises and covers normally dry land, from heavy rain, an overflowing river or a storm surge. It needs a separate flood insurance policy.
INS-08.Earthquake: Damage from the ground shaking. It is left out of a standard policy and has to be added as an endorsement or bought as a separate policy.
INS-08.Wear and tear: The gradual aging of a home and its parts, such as an old roof wearing out. Insurance covers sudden accidents, not the normal cost of things getting old.
INS-08.Pest damage: Harm done by termites, rodents, insects and similar animals. Insurers treat it as a preventable upkeep problem, so it is excluded.
INS-08.Mold: Fungus that grows where moisture lingers. It is generally excluded, especially when it comes from long-term dampness or a leak the owner did not fix.
INS-08.Poor maintenance: Damage that happens because the owner failed to look after the home, such as ignoring a failing roof. The policy expects owners to keep the property in repair.
INS-08.Intentional damage: Loss that the policyholder causes on purpose, such as setting fire to the home. Insurance never pays people for damage they deliberately do to their own property.
INS-08.Sewer backup: Water that comes back up through a drain or sewer line or overflows from a sump pump. It is excluded unless the owner adds water backup coverage.
INS-08.Landslide or mudslide: Kinds of earth movement, along with sinkholes. A standard policy excludes damage caused by the ground shifting or sliding.
INS-08.Slow leaks: Water that seeps or drips over weeks or months. A sudden burst pipe is covered, but damage from a leak that went on for a long time is not.
INS-08.War: Damage caused by war or military action. Losses of this kind are too large and widespread to insure, so every standard policy excludes them.
INS-08.Nuclear hazard: Damage from a nuclear reaction, radiation or radioactive contamination, which standard homeowners policies exclude.
INS-08.Home business losses: Losses tied to a business run from the home. Business equipment gets only a small amount of coverage and business lawsuits are excluded, so separate coverage is needed.
INS-08.Cars and other motor vehicles: Damage to or theft of a car, even when it is parked in the garage at home. Vehicles are covered by an auto policy, not a homeowners policy.
INS-08.Government action: The seizure or destruction of property by order of a government authority, such as condemning a building. It is a standard exclusion.
INS-08.Ordinance or law: The extra cost of rebuilding to meet current building codes after a loss. A standard policy pays little or none of it unless coverage is added.
INS-08.Power failure: Loss caused by an electricity outage that starts away from the home, such as food spoiling in the freezer. A standard policy excludes it.
INS-08.Faulty workmanship: Damage that results from poor construction, bad design or defective materials. The policy does not pay to fix a builder's mistakes.
INS-08.Settling or cracking: The slow settling, shrinking, bulging or cracking of foundations, walls and floors as a house ages, which is excluded.
INS-08.Damage by your own pets: Harm that an animal you own does to your home or belongings, such as a dog chewing the furniture. Standard policies exclude it.

INS-09.Raise the deductible: Agreeing to pay more of each loss yourself before the insurer pays. The insurer takes on less risk, so it charges a lower premium.
INS-09.Shop around: Getting price quotes from several insurers for the same coverage. Prices for the same person can differ widely from one company to another.
INS-09.Bundle policies: Buying more than one policy, such as home and auto, from the same insurer. Most insurers give a discount for it.
INS-09.Drive safely: Keeping a record free of accidents and traffic tickets. Insurers charge less to drivers who have shown they are less likely to make a claim.
INS-09.Ask for discounts: Checking which price reductions the insurer offers and making sure every one you qualify for is applied to your policy.
INS-09.Reduce coverage: Removing coverage you do not need or choosing lower limits, such as dropping collision on an old car. It saves money but leaves you paying more after a loss.
INS-09.Improve your credit: Raising your credit standing by paying bills on time and keeping debt low. In most states insurers may use credit history when they price auto and home policies.
INS-09.Good student discount: A lower auto premium that many insurers give to young drivers who keep high grades in school.
INS-09.Take a defensive driving course: Completing an approved class on safe driving. Many insurers lower the auto premium for drivers who finish one.
INS-09.Install safety or security devices: Adding equipment that makes a loss less likely, such as smoke detectors, a burglar alarm or an anti-theft device in a car.
INS-09.Drive less: Putting fewer miles on the car each year. Less time on the road means less chance of an accident, so many insurers charge low-mileage drivers less.
INS-09.Choose a car that costs less to insure: Picking a vehicle that is cheaper to repair, safer in a crash and stolen less often. Checking insurance prices before buying can save money every year.
INS-09.Pay the premium in full: Paying for the whole policy period at once instead of monthly. It avoids installment fees and often earns a discount.
INS-09.Healthy lifestyle: Habits such as not smoking that lower health risks. Non-smokers pay much less for life insurance, and some health plans reward wellness programs.
INS-09.Usage-based insurance: An auto program that uses an app or device, called telematics, to track how and how much you drive. Careful or low-mileage drivers earn a lower price.
INS-09.Use group insurance: Buying coverage through an employer or another organization. Group rates are often lower than buying alone, and an employer may pay part of the premium.
INS-09.Autopay or paperless billing: Letting the insurer take payments automatically and send bills electronically. Many insurers give a small discount for each.
INS-09.Stay with one insurer: Keeping a policy with the same company for years. Some insurers reward long-term customers with a loyalty or renewal discount.
INS-09.Avoid small claims: Paying for minor damage yourself instead of filing a claim. A record with few claims can earn a discount and helps keep the premium from rising.
INS-09.Stay on a family policy: Remaining on a parent's policy instead of buying your own. For a young driver it usually costs far less than a separate auto policy.
INS-09.Buy life insurance while young: Taking out life insurance at a young age and in good health. The premium is based largely on age and health when you buy, so it starts lower.
INS-09.Maintain continuous coverage: Keeping insurance in force with no gaps. Insurers often charge more to drivers whose coverage has lapsed.

INS-10.Social Security: The federal program, paid for by a payroll tax on workers and employers, that pays monthly income to retired workers, disabled workers and the families of workers who have died.
INS-10.Medicare: The federal health insurance program for people 65 and older and for some younger people with disabilities, funded partly by a payroll tax.
INS-10.Medicaid: Public health coverage for people with low incomes, paid for jointly by the federal government and the states and run by each state.
INS-10.Unemployment insurance: A program run by the states with federal oversight that pays temporary income to workers who lose a job through no fault of their own. Employers pay the taxes that fund it.
INS-10.FDIC deposit insurance: Protection from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, a federal agency. If an insured bank fails, depositors get their money back up to a legal limit.
INS-10.Workers compensation: Insurance required by state law that pays medical bills and part of lost wages when an employee is hurt or made ill by the job. Employers pay for it.
INS-10.Social Security Disability Insurance: The part of Social Security that pays monthly benefits to people who have worked and paid into the system but can no longer work because of a serious disability.
INS-10.CHIP: The Children's Health Insurance Program, run by the states with federal money. It covers children in families that earn too much for Medicaid but cannot afford private plans.
INS-10.National Flood Insurance Program: A federal program that offers flood insurance to owners and renters in participating communities, because standard homeowners policies exclude floods.
