INS-10.NCUA share insurance: Protection from the National Credit Union Administration, a federal agency. It covers deposits at insured credit unions the way the FDIC covers bank deposits.
INS-10.Federal crop insurance: A federal program that helps farmers buy insurance against losing a crop to weather or disease, or against a drop in crop prices.
INS-10.TRICARE: The federal health care program for military service members, military retirees and their families.
INS-10.Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation: A federal agency that insures traditional private pension plans. If a covered plan cannot pay, it pays retirees their benefits up to a legal limit.
INS-10.Servicemembers Group Life Insurance: Low-cost life insurance that the federal government offers to members of the military. Veterans can continue coverage under a related program after leaving the service.
INS-10.FHA mortgage insurance: Insurance from the Federal Housing Administration that repays the lender if a home buyer defaults. It lets lenders approve buyers with small down payments.
INS-10.State disability insurance: A program in a few states, funded by payroll deductions, that replaces part of a worker's wages during an illness or injury that is not related to the job.
INS-10.Paid family leave insurance: A program in some states, funded by payroll contributions, that replaces part of a worker's pay during time off to care for a new child or a seriously ill relative.
INS-10.Railroad Retirement: A separate federal program that provides retirement, disability and survivor benefits to railroad workers and their families in place of Social Security.

CRD-08.Pay bills on time: Making at least the required payment by every due date. Payment history is the biggest part of a credit score, so this matters more than anything else.
CRD-08.Get a credit card and use it responsibly: Opening a card, charging only what you can afford and paying the bill on time. It creates the record of borrowing and repaying that lenders look for.
CRD-08.Keep balances low: Using only a small share of your credit limits. A low credit utilization, the balance divided by the limit, shows you are not relying heavily on borrowed money.
CRD-08.Pay off debt: Reducing what you owe on cards and loans. Lower balances improve the amounts-owed part of a credit score.
CRD-08.Pay the full balance each month: Paying the whole statement balance, not just the minimum. It avoids interest and keeps the balance reported to the credit bureaus low.
CRD-08.Get a secured credit card: A card backed by a cash deposit that usually sets the credit limit. It is easier to get with no credit history, and the payments are reported to the credit bureaus.
CRD-08.Become an authorized user: Being added to another person's credit card account, often a parent's. The account's history can appear on your credit report and help your score.
CRD-08.Check your credit report for errors: Reading your credit report and disputing anything wrong, such as an account that is not yours. Removing a mistake can raise your score.
CRD-08.Limit new credit applications: Applying for credit only when you need it. Each application can cause a hard inquiry, and several in a short time can lower your score.
CRD-08.Keep old accounts open: Leaving your oldest accounts open, even if you rarely use them. They lengthen your credit history and keep your available credit higher.
CRD-08.Credit-builder loan: A small loan designed for building credit. The lender holds the money in an account while you make payments, then releases it to you at the end.
CRD-08.Take out a loan and repay it: Borrowing a fixed amount and making every scheduled payment. A well-paid installment loan adds positive history to your credit report.
CRD-08.Have a mix of credit types: Handling both revolving credit, such as a credit card, and installment credit, such as a car loan. Credit mix is a small part of a credit score.
CRD-08.Get a cosigner: Asking someone with good credit to sign a loan with you and promise to pay if you do not. It can help you get approved so you can build your own record.
CRD-08.Set up automatic payments: Having payments taken from your bank account on schedule, so a due date is never missed by accident.
CRD-08.Ask for a higher credit limit: Requesting a larger limit on a card. If your spending stays the same, the balance becomes a smaller share of the limit, which lowers your utilization.
CRD-08.Store credit card: A card from a retailer that works only at that store. It is often easier to qualify for, and paying it on time builds credit history.
CRD-08.Report rent and utility payments: Using a service that sends your on-time rent or utility payments to the credit bureaus, since these bills do not normally appear on a credit report.
CRD-08.Bring past-due accounts current: Catching up on any payments you have missed. An account that is behind keeps hurting your credit until it is brought up to date.
CRD-08.Work with a credit counselor: Getting help from a nonprofit credit counseling agency, which can review your finances and set up a plan for paying down debt.

CRD-09.Lower credit score: Late payments and defaults are reported to the credit bureaus and can stay on a credit report for years, pulling the score down.
CRD-09.Late fees: Charges the lender adds each time a payment arrives after the due date, which make the debt more expensive.
CRD-09.Repossession: The lender takes back property that secured the loan, most often a car, and sells it to recover what is owed.
CRD-09.Foreclosure: The legal process in which a mortgage lender takes a home and sells it because the borrower stopped making payments.
CRD-09.Debt sent to collections: The lender hands or sells the unpaid debt to a collection agency, which then contacts the borrower to demand payment. It appears on the credit report.
CRD-09.Higher interest rates: A card issuer can apply a higher penalty rate after late payments, and lenders charge more on future loans to borrowers with a poor record.
CRD-09.More interest owed: Interest keeps being added to the unpaid balance, so the total owed grows the longer payments are missed.
CRD-09.Harder to get future credit: Lenders see the missed payments on the credit report and may turn down later applications for loans or credit cards.
CRD-09.Lawsuit: The lender or a collector can sue for the unpaid amount. If it wins, the court issues a judgment ordering the borrower to pay.
CRD-09.Wage garnishment: An order, usually from a court, that makes an employer send part of the borrower's paycheck straight to the creditor.
CRD-09.Bankruptcy: A legal process for people who cannot pay their debts. It can cancel or reorganize what is owed, but it stays on a credit report for years.
CRD-09.Account closed or credit limit cut: A card issuer can lower the credit limit, suspend the card or close the account when the borrower falls behind.
CRD-09.Charge-off: The lender gives up on collecting and writes the debt off as a loss. The borrower still owes it, and the charge-off is a serious negative mark on a credit report.
CRD-09.Lien on property: A legal claim placed on something the borrower owns, such as a house. The property cannot be sold with a clear title until the debt is paid.
CRD-09.Cosigner held responsible: Anyone who cosigned promised to pay if the borrower did not. The lender can demand payment from the cosigner, and the cosigner's credit is damaged too.
CRD-09.Trouble renting or getting hired: Landlords and some employers check credit reports. A record of unpaid debt can lead them to turn an applicant down.
CRD-09.Acceleration of the loan: Under an acceleration clause, the lender can demand the entire remaining balance at once after a default, not just the missed payments.
CRD-09.Bank account levy: After winning a court judgment, a creditor can have money taken directly from the borrower's bank account to pay the debt.
CRD-09.Tax refund withheld: For debts owed to the government, such as defaulted federal student loans, the borrower's income tax refund can be kept and applied to the debt.
CRD-09.Higher insurance premiums: In most states insurers may use credit history in pricing, so damaged credit can raise the cost of auto and home insurance.
CRD-09.Deficiency balance: The amount still owed when repossessed or foreclosed property sells for less than the debt. The lender can pursue the borrower for the difference.

CRD-10.Rewards card: A card that gives something back for spending, such as points that can be traded for merchandise, travel or statement credits.
CRD-10.Cash back card: A rewards card that returns a small percentage of each purchase to the cardholder as money, usually as a statement credit or deposit.
CRD-10.Travel card: A rewards card that earns airline miles, hotel points or general travel points, often with extras such as free checked bags or travel insurance.
CRD-10.Student card: A card made for college students with little or no credit history. It usually has a low credit limit and is easier to qualify for.
CRD-10.Store card: A card issued for one retailer. Many work only at that store, and they tend to offer store discounts but charge high interest rates.
CRD-10.Secured card: A card backed by a cash deposit that usually equals the credit limit. It is meant for people who are building or rebuilding credit.
CRD-10.Business card: A credit card for a business owner to pay company expenses, which keeps business spending separate from personal spending.
CRD-10.Balance transfer card: A card that lets you move debt from other cards onto it, usually at a low or zero introductory interest rate, to pay the debt down faster.
CRD-10.Low-interest card: A card whose main feature is a lower ongoing interest rate than most cards, which helps people who sometimes carry a balance.
CRD-10.Zero percent intro APR card: A card that charges no interest for an introductory period. APR means annual percentage rate, and the normal rate applies once the period ends.
CRD-10.Standard card: A basic unsecured credit card with no deposit required and no rewards program. It simply offers a line of credit to borrow against and repay.
CRD-10.No-annual-fee card: A card that does not charge a yearly fee just for having the account, so it costs nothing to keep if the balance is paid in full.
CRD-10.Charge card: A card with no preset spending limit whose balance must be paid in full every month, so it cannot be used to carry debt over time.
CRD-10.Premium card: A high-end card with a large annual fee that offers richer rewards and perks, such as airport lounge access and travel credits.
CRD-10.Co-branded card: A card that a bank issues in partnership with another company, such as an airline or retailer, and that earns rewards with that company.
CRD-10.Gas card: A card issued by or for a fuel company that gives discounts or rewards on gasoline. Some can be used only at that brand of station.
CRD-10.Credit-builder card: A starter card for people with poor or no credit. It has a low limit and often higher costs, and it reports payments to the credit bureaus.
CRD-10.Corporate card: A card that a larger company gives employees for approved business expenses. The company, not the employee, is usually responsible for paying the bill.
CRD-10.Affinity card: A card linked to an organization such as a charity, university or sports team. The issuer gives the organization a small share of what cardholders spend.
CRD-10.Virtual card: A card number created for online use with no physical card. It can be limited to one merchant or one purchase to reduce the risk of fraud.

CRD-11.Paying only the minimum: Sending just the smallest payment the card issuer allows. Most of it goes to interest, so the balance hardly falls and the debt can last for many years.
CRD-11.Missing or late payments: Bills are paid after the due date or not at all because there is not enough money to cover them. It is one of the clearest signs that debt is out of hand.
CRD-11.Maxed-out credit cards: Card balances are at or close to the credit limit, leaving nothing in reserve. It shows heavy reliance on borrowing and also lowers a credit score.
CRD-11.Borrowing to pay other debts: Taking a new loan or using one credit card to make the payments on another. The total owed does not shrink, and added interest and fees make it grow.
CRD-11.Using credit for everyday needs: Charging basics such as groceries, gas or rent because there is no cash to pay for them, without being able to pay the card off at the end of the month.
CRD-11.Calls from debt collectors: Lenders or collection agencies phone or write to demand overdue payments. By this point accounts are seriously behind.
CRD-11.No savings: So much income goes to debt payments that nothing can be set aside. Without an emergency fund, any surprise expense has to go on credit too.
CRD-11.High debt-to-income ratio: Monthly debt payments divided by monthly income. When payments take up a large share of each paycheck, there is too little left for living costs.
CRD-11.Being denied credit: A lender turns down an application for a loan or card. Lenders refuse when a credit report shows that a person already owes too much or pays late.
CRD-11.Balances that keep growing: The total owed is higher each month even though payments are being made, because new charges and interest are added faster than the debt is paid off.
CRD-11.Falling credit score: A credit score that keeps dropping. High balances and late payments are the two things that pull a score down the most.
CRD-11.Taking cash advances: Borrowing cash against a credit card to cover expenses. Advances carry a fee and a higher interest rate that starts at once, so they are a costly last resort.
CRD-11.Not knowing how much you owe: Losing track of the total owed, or leaving bills unopened to avoid seeing it. Someone in control of their debt can say roughly what they owe and to whom.
CRD-11.Using payday loans: Turning to very short-term loans with extremely high costs in order to reach the next paycheck. People who rely on them often end up borrowing again and again.
CRD-11.Dipping into savings or retirement funds: Using long-term savings or retirement money to pay regular bills or debt payments. It solves the problem for a month but gives up future security.
CRD-11.Overdrawing your bank account: Spending more than the checking account holds, often and not by accident. Repeated overdrafts show that income is not covering the bills.
CRD-11.Stress or arguments about money: Constant worry about bills, quarrels at home over spending, or hiding purchases and balances from family members.
CRD-11.Juggling bills: Paying some bills this month and putting off others because there is not enough money to pay them all, then switching which ones are skipped next month.
CRD-11.Borrowing from family or friends: Regularly asking relatives or friends for money to cover bills or payments, a sign that normal income and credit have run out.
CRD-11.Repeated balance transfers: Moving debt from card to card over and over to chase a low introductory rate without ever paying the balance down.
CRD-11.Applying for new credit to keep up: Opening new cards or asking for higher limits because the existing ones are full, which adds room to borrow without fixing the cause.
CRD-11.Working extra hours just to make payment: Depending on overtime or a second job only to keep up with debt payments, so that any loss of those extra hours would mean missed payments.

BNK-08.Fees: What the bank charges for an account and its services, such as a monthly maintenance fee. Some accounts have none, so comparing fee schedules saves money.
BNK-08.Interest rates: What the bank pays on money you deposit. Compare the annual percentage yield (APY), which shows how much a balance earns in a year with compounding included.
BNK-08.Branch locations: How close the bank's offices are to where you live, work or study, which matters if you want to deposit cash or talk to someone in person.
BNK-08.ATM access: How many cash machines you can use without paying a fee, and where they are. Using a machine outside the bank's network usually costs extra.
BNK-08.Online and mobile banking: The quality of the bank's website and app, including features such as depositing a check with your phone, paying bills and sending money.
BNK-08.Minimum balance requirement: The amount you must deposit to open the account or keep in it to avoid a fee. A high minimum can make an account a poor fit.
BNK-08.Customer service: How easy it is to get help by phone, online or in a branch, and how well the staff solve problems when something goes wrong.
BNK-08.Deposit insurance: Whether accounts are covered by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) or, at a credit union, the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) if the institution fails.
BNK-08.Products and services offered: The range of accounts and services available, such as checking, savings, loans and credit cards, so that your needs can be met in one place.
BNK-08.Overdraft policy: What happens if you spend more than your balance: whether the payment is declined or covered, and what fee, if any, the bank charges.
BNK-08.Reputation: What customers and independent reviews say about the bank, including how stable it is and how fairly it treats people.
BNK-08.Hours of operation: When branches and phone support are open, for example evenings or weekends, which matters if you cannot visit during the working day.
BNK-08.Security features: The tools a bank uses to protect an account, such as fraud monitoring, account alerts and a second sign-in step.
BNK-08.Sign-up bonus: Cash or another reward some banks give new customers for opening an account and meeting conditions such as setting up direct deposit.
BNK-08.Loan rates: The interest the bank charges borrowers on car loans, mortgages and credit cards, which matters if you expect to borrow from it later.
BNK-08.Type of institution: Whether it is a traditional bank, an online-only bank or a credit union. Each tends to differ in fees, interest rates and the personal service it offers.
BNK-08.Withdrawal or transaction limits: Caps on how much cash you can take out or how many transfers you can make in a day or month, which vary by bank and account.
BNK-08.Funds availability: How soon after a deposit you can use the money. Some banks hold checks longer than others, and some release direct deposits early.
BNK-08.Rewards or perks: Extras attached to an account, such as cash back on debit card purchases, free checks or refunds of other banks' ATM fees.
BNK-08.Membership requirements: The rules about who may join. Credit unions serve only members, who qualify through an employer, a community or another shared link.

BNK-09.Ending balance: The amount in the account on the last day the statement covers, after every deposit, withdrawal and fee for the period.
BNK-09.Deposits: Money added to the account during the period, such as paychecks sent by direct deposit, cash and checks. The statement lists each one and often a total.
BNK-09.Withdrawals: Money taken out of the account during the period, including cash from an ATM. Statements often group these with other debits and show a total.
BNK-09.Transactions: The itemized list of everything that moved money in or out, such as debit card purchases, each with a date, a short description and an amount.
BNK-09.Account number: The number that identifies your account at the bank. Many statements print only the last few digits to protect against fraud.
BNK-09.Beginning balance: The amount in the account at the start of the period, which equals the ending balance of the previous statement.
BNK-09.Fees: Charges the bank took from the account during the period, such as a monthly maintenance fee or an overdraft fee.
BNK-09.Interest earned: The amount the bank added to the account during the period as payment for holding your money, shown on accounts that pay interest.
BNK-09.Account holder name and address: The name of the person or people who own the account and the mailing address the bank has on file.
BNK-09.Statement period: The first and last dates the statement covers, usually about one month. Only transactions inside those dates appear on it.
BNK-09.Transaction dates: The day each item was made or was posted to the account, which helps you match the statement against your own records.
BNK-09.Checks paid: The checks you wrote that the bank has paid from the account, listed by check number and amount, sometimes with small pictures of them.
BNK-09.Bank name and contact information: The name of the bank and how to reach it, including a phone number and address for questions about the statement.
BNK-09.Electronic transfers: Money moved in or out without paper, such as automatic bill payments and transfers between accounts through the ACH network.
BNK-09.Account type: The kind of account the statement is for, such as checking or savings, often shown with the name the bank gives that product.
BNK-09.Account summary: A short box, usually near the top, that totals the period: beginning balance, total deposits, total withdrawals, fees and ending balance.
BNK-09.Daily balance summary: A table showing the balance in the account at the end of each day on which it changed during the period.
BNK-09.Average daily balance: The sum of each day's balance divided by the number of days in the period. Banks use it to work out interest or to decide whether a fee applies.
BNK-09.Annual percentage yield earned: The yearly rate of return the account actually earned for the period, with compounding included. Statements for interest-bearing accounts must show it.
BNK-09.Year-to-date interest: The total interest the account has earned since January 1, which is useful at tax time because interest counts as income.
BNK-09.Error reporting instructions: A notice explaining how to tell the bank about a mistake or an unauthorized transaction, and how quickly you must report it.

BNK-10.Interest on loans: What borrowers pay the bank for the use of its money on mortgages, car loans, business loans and other lending. It is the largest source of income for most banks.
BNK-10.Account fees: Charges for holding and using a deposit account, such as a monthly maintenance fee. Banks often waive them for customers who keep a minimum balance.
BNK-10.Credit card interest and fees: Interest charged on card balances that are not paid in full, plus annual fees and other card charges. Card rates are among the highest a bank charges.
BNK-10.Overdraft fees: Charges applied when a customer spends more than the account holds and the bank covers or returns the payment.
BNK-10.Investing deposits: Banks put money they do not lend out into investments such as U.S. Treasury securities and other bonds, and earn interest on them.
BNK-10.ATM fees: Charges collected when people who are not the bank's customers use its cash machines, or when its own customers use machines outside its network.
BNK-10.Late fees: Penalties charged when a borrower or cardholder misses a payment due date.
BNK-10.Net interest spread: The gap between the interest rate a bank earns on loans and the rate it pays on deposits. Lending at a higher rate than it pays savers is the core of banking.
BNK-10.Interchange fees: A small percentage of each card purchase paid to the bank that issued the card. The cost falls on the merchant and is often called a swipe fee.
BNK-10.Loan origination fees: Upfront charges for processing and setting up a new loan, common on mortgages, collected in addition to the interest.
BNK-10.Wealth management fees: Charges for managing customers' investments, giving financial advice and running trusts, usually set as a percentage of the money being managed.
BNK-10.Wire transfer fees: Charges for sending or receiving money by wire, a fast electronic transfer between banks.
BNK-10.Foreign exchange fees: Income from converting one currency into another, earned through a fee or by giving customers a slightly less favorable exchange rate.
BNK-10.Investment banking fees: Payments large banks earn for helping companies issue stocks and bonds, which is called underwriting, and for advising on mergers.
BNK-10.Trading: Profits some large banks make by buying and selling securities, currencies and other financial instruments, often on behalf of clients.
BNK-10.Safe deposit box rental: Yearly rent customers pay for a locked box in the bank's vault where they keep documents and valuables.
BNK-10.Selling loans: Banks often sell loans they have made, especially mortgages, to investors. They can earn a gain on the sale and free up money to lend again.
BNK-10.Loan servicing fees: Payments a bank earns for collecting monthly payments and handling the paperwork on loans, including loans it has sold to investors.
BNK-10.Insurance sales: Commissions a bank earns when it sells insurance policies or annuities to its customers, usually on behalf of an insurance company.
BNK-10.Treasury and cash management services: Fees businesses pay a bank to help collect payments, pay bills and manage their daily cash balances.
BNK-10.Interest on reserves: Interest that the Federal Reserve pays banks on the balances they keep on deposit with it.

BNK-11.Federal Reserve: The central bank of the United States. Besides setting monetary policy, it supervises bank holding companies and many state-chartered banks.
BNK-11.Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation: The FDIC insures deposits at member banks up to a legal limit, supervises many state-chartered banks and takes over banks that fail.
BNK-11.Securities and Exchange Commission: The SEC is the federal agency that regulates the stock and bond markets, requires public companies to disclose financial information and enforces laws against securities fraud.
BNK-11.Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: The CFPB is a federal agency created after the 2008 financial crisis to write and enforce rules for consumer products such as mortgages, credit cards and student loans.
BNK-11.Department of the Treasury: The federal department that manages the government's money and debt. Several financial regulators, including the OCC and FinCEN, are bureaus within it.
BNK-11.Federal Trade Commission: The FTC enforces consumer protection laws against unfair or deceptive practices, including those of non-bank lenders, debt collectors and credit bureaus.
BNK-11.Office of the Comptroller of the Currenc: The OCC is the bureau of the Treasury Department that charters, regulates and supervises national banks and federal savings associations.
BNK-11.National Credit Union Administration: The NCUA is the federal agency that charters and supervises federal credit unions and insures deposits at credit unions.
BNK-11.FINRA: The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority is not a government agency. It is a self-regulatory body, overseen by the SEC, that licenses and polices brokers and brokerage firms.
BNK-11.State banking regulators: Agencies in each state that charter and examine state banks and license other lenders, such as mortgage companies and payday lenders.
BNK-11.Commodity Futures Trading Commission: The CFTC is the federal agency that regulates the markets for futures, options on futures and swaps.
BNK-11.State insurance commissioners: Insurance is regulated mainly by the states. Each state's insurance department licenses insurers and agents, reviews rates and handles consumer complaints.
BNK-11.Federal Housing Finance Agency: The FHFA is the federal agency that oversees Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks, which supply much of the money for U.S. mortgages.
BNK-11.Financial Crimes Enforcement Network: FinCEN is a Treasury bureau that fights money laundering. Banks must report suspicious activity and large cash transactions to it.
BNK-11.Financial Stability Oversight Council: The FSOC is a council of the heads of the main financial regulators, chaired by the Treasury Secretary, that watches for risks to the whole financial system.
BNK-11.Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board: The MSRB is a self-regulatory body, overseen by the SEC, that writes the rules for firms that sell and trade municipal bonds.
BNK-11.State securities regulators: State agencies that register smaller securities offerings, license brokers and advisers in the state and investigate investment fraud.
BNK-11.Public Company Accounting Oversight Boar: The PCAOB is a board created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and overseen by the SEC. It inspects and sets standards for the firms that audit public companies.
BNK-11.Department of Housing and Urban Developm: HUD is the federal department that includes the Federal Housing Administration, which insures mortgages. HUD also enforces fair housing rules in home lending.
BNK-11.Farm Credit Administration: The federal agency that regulates the Farm Credit System, a network of lenders that serves farmers, ranchers and rural communities.
BNK-11.Department of Labor: The federal department that oversees most employer retirement plans, such as 401(k) plans, and the people who manage them.

INV-08.Price: What one share most recently sold for. It is the headline number in a quote and changes throughout the trading day.
INV-08.Ticker symbol: The short code of letters that identifies a stock on an exchange, such as AAPL for Apple.
INV-08.Company name: The full name of the business that issued the stock, shown next to its ticker symbol.
INV-08.Change: How much the price has risen or fallen since the previous close, shown in dollars and as a percentage.
INV-08.Volume: The number of shares that have changed hands during the day. High volume means the stock is being traded heavily.
INV-08.52-week high and low: The highest and lowest prices the stock has traded at over the past year, which show where today's price sits in its recent range.
INV-08.Day high and low: The highest and lowest prices the stock has traded at so far in the current trading day.
INV-08.Opening price: The price of the first trade when the market opened for the day.
INV-08.Previous close: The price of the last trade on the day before. Today's change is measured against it.
INV-08.Market capitalization: The total value of all of a company's shares: the share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding.
INV-08.P/E ratio: The price-to-earnings ratio is the share price divided by earnings per share. It shows how much investors pay for each dollar of profit.
INV-08.Dividend: The cash the company pays its shareholders for each share they own, usually stated as a yearly amount.
INV-08.Dividend yield: The annual dividend per share divided by the share price, shown as a percentage. It tells you the income return from dividends alone.
INV-08.Bid and ask prices: The bid is the highest price a buyer is currently offering and the ask is the lowest price a seller will accept. The gap between them is the spread.
INV-08.Earnings per share: The company's profit divided by its number of shares outstanding, usually for the past twelve months.
INV-08.Exchange: The market where the stock is listed and traded, such as the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq.
INV-08.Price chart: A graph of the stock's price over a chosen time, from a single day to several years, that makes trends easy to see.
INV-08.Beta: A measure of how much the stock tends to move compared with the market as a whole. A beta above 1 means it has swung more than the market.
INV-08.Ex-dividend date: The cutoff date for the next dividend. Someone who buys the stock on or after this date does not receive that payment.
INV-08.Earnings date: The day the company is expected to announce its next quarterly results, when its stock price often moves sharply.
INV-08.Analyst price target: The price that professional analysts who follow the company expect the stock to reach, usually within about a year.
INV-08.Time of last trade: The date and time of the most recent trade or price update, which tells you how current the quote is.
INV-08.Shares outstanding: The total number of the company's shares held by all investors. Multiplying it by the share price gives the market capitalization.
INV-08.After-hours price: The price in trading that takes place before the market opens or after it closes, when fewer shares change hands.

INV-09.Common stock: The basic form of ownership in a corporation. Holders usually get a vote and may receive dividends, but they are paid last if the company fails.
INV-09.Preferred stock: Shares that pay a fixed dividend before common shareholders receive anything and rank ahead of them if the company fails. They usually carry no vote.
INV-09.Blue chip stock: Stock of a large, well-known, financially strong company with a long record of steady earnings and, often, regular dividends.
INV-09.Growth stock: Stock of a company whose sales and profits are expected to grow faster than average. It usually pays little or no dividend because profits are reinvested.
INV-09.Penny stock: A very low-priced stock of a small company, often traded outside the major exchanges. It is risky and can be hard to sell.
INV-09.Dividend stock: Also called an income stock. It belongs to a company that pays regular, relatively high dividends, so investors hold it for steady income.
INV-09.Value stock: A stock that looks cheap compared with the company's earnings or assets. Investors buy it expecting the market to recognize its worth later.
INV-09.Large-cap stock: Stock of a company with a large market capitalization, the total value of all its shares. These are the biggest companies and tend to be more stable.
INV-09.Mid-cap stock: Stock of a medium-sized company, between the large and small groups when measured by market capitalization, the total value of its shares.
INV-09.Small-cap stock: Stock of a smaller company measured by market capitalization. It has more room to grow than a giant but its price tends to swing more.
INV-09.Cyclical stock: Stock of a company whose profits rise and fall with the economy, such as an automaker or airline. It does well in booms and poorly in recessions.
INV-09.Defensive stock: Stock of a company that sells things people buy in good times and bad, such as food or electricity, so its earnings hold up in a downturn.
INV-09.International stock: Stock of a company based outside the investor's home country. It adds diversification but brings currency risk and political risk.
INV-09.Speculative stock: A high-risk stock bought in the hope of a big gain, often in a company with little or no profit, where a large loss is also possible.
INV-09.IPO stock: Shares sold to the public for the first time in an initial public offering, when a private company lists on a stock exchange.
INV-09.Class A or Class B shares: Different classes of a company's common stock that carry different voting rights. Founders often keep the class with more votes per share.
INV-09.Treasury stock: Shares a company once issued and has since bought back. They are held by the company itself, have no vote and receive no dividends.
INV-09.Restricted stock: Shares given to employees or insiders that cannot be sold until conditions are met, such as staying with the company for a set number of years.
INV-09.Cumulative or convertible preferred stoc: Kinds of preferred stock. Cumulative preferred must be paid any skipped dividends before common holders get anything, and convertible preferred can be exchanged for common shares.
INV-09.American depositary receipt: A certificate that trades on a U.S. market and stands for shares of a foreign company, letting Americans invest in it in dollars.
INV-09.Over-the-counter stock: Stock that is not listed on an exchange and trades through a network of dealers. Many are small companies with lighter reporting requirements.
INV-09.Authorized, issued or outstanding shares: A classification by status: authorized shares are the most a company may issue, issued shares have been sold, and outstanding shares are those investors still hold.
INV-09.Par value or no-par stock: Par value is a small face amount per share stated in the corporate charter and used in the accounting records. No-par stock has no such stated amount.

INV-10.Buy and hold: Buying investments and keeping them for many years, through ups and downs, instead of trading often. It relies on markets rising over the long run.
INV-10.Diversification: Spreading money across many different investments so that a loss in one has only a small effect on the whole portfolio.
INV-10.Day trading: Buying and selling within the same day to profit from small price moves. It is very risky, and most people who try it lose money.
INV-10.Index investing: Buying funds that copy a market index, such as the S&P 500, instead of trying to beat it. It is called passive investing and has low costs.
INV-10.Dollar-cost averaging: Investing the same amount of money at regular intervals whatever the price. You buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when they are high.
INV-10.Value investing: Looking for stocks that sell for less than the company appears to be worth, then waiting for the price to catch up.
INV-10.Growth investing: Buying shares of companies expected to grow their sales and profits quickly, even if the stock looks expensive today.
INV-10.Dividend investing: Choosing stocks that pay regular dividends, in order to collect a steady income as well as any rise in the share price.
INV-10.Short selling: Selling borrowed shares in the hope of buying them back later at a lower price. The seller profits if the price falls and loses if it rises.
INV-10.Asset allocation: Deciding what share of a portfolio goes into each type of asset, such as stocks, bonds and cash, based on your goals, time frame and comfort with risk.
INV-10.Market timing: Trying to buy just before prices rise and sell just before they fall. It is very hard to do consistently, even for professionals.
INV-10.Active investing: Picking individual investments and trading them in an attempt to beat the market, instead of simply matching an index.
INV-10.Swing trading: Holding a position for a few days or weeks to profit from a short-term price swing. It sits between day trading and long-term investing.
INV-10.Momentum investing: Buying investments that have been rising, and selling those that have been falling, on the idea that recent trends tend to continue for a while.
INV-10.Rebalancing: Selling some of what has grown and buying more of what has lagged, to bring a portfolio back to its planned mix of assets.
INV-10.Dividend reinvestment: Using dividends to buy more shares automatically instead of taking the cash, which lets the investment compound. A plan that does this is called a DRIP.
INV-10.Hedging: Making a second investment that should gain if the first one loses, such as buying a put option on a stock you own, to limit possible losses.
INV-10.Buying on margin: Borrowing money from a broker to buy more securities than your own cash allows. It magnifies both gains and losses.
INV-10.Options trading: Using contracts that give the right to buy or sell a stock at a set price by a set date, either to speculate or to protect or earn income on shares you own.
INV-10.Technical analysis: Choosing when to buy and sell by studying charts of past prices and trading volume, looking for patterns and trends.
INV-10.Fundamental analysis: Choosing investments by studying a company's financial statements, management and industry to estimate what it is really worth.
INV-10.Contrarian investing: Going against the crowd: buying what most investors are selling and selling what they are eagerly buying.
INV-10.Tax-loss harvesting: Selling an investment that has dropped in value so the loss can be used to reduce the tax owed on gains from other investments.
INV-10.Laddering: Buying bonds or certificates of deposit that mature at evenly spaced dates. Money comes due regularly and can be reinvested at current rates.
INV-10.Socially responsible investing: Choosing investments by ethical, environmental or social standards as well as by expected return. It is also known as ESG investing.
INV-10.Scalping: A very short-term trading style that makes many trades a day, each aiming for a tiny profit from a small price change.
INV-10.Arbitrage: Buying something in one market and selling it at almost the same moment in another market where the price is higher, to lock in the difference.

INV-11.Commission: A charge a broker collects for carrying out a trade. Many online brokers no longer charge it on stock trades, but it still applies to some investments.
INV-11.Taxes: Profit from selling an investment for more than it cost is taxed as a capital gain, and dividends and interest are taxed as income.
INV-11.Management fee: What an adviser or money manager charges for choosing and overseeing your investments, usually a yearly percentage of the amount being managed.
INV-11.Account maintenance fee: A flat charge some brokers and retirement plan providers collect each year just for keeping the account open.
INV-11.Expense ratio: A fund's yearly operating costs divided by its assets. A ratio of one percent means one dollar of every hundred invested goes to costs each year.
INV-11.Sales load: A sales charge on some mutual funds that pays the broker who sold them. A front-end load is taken when you buy and a back-end load when you sell.
INV-11.Bid-ask spread: The gap between the price buyers are offering and the price sellers are asking. An investor who buys and then sells at once loses this difference.
INV-11.Margin interest: Interest a broker charges on money lent to an investor to buy securities. It adds up for as long as the loan is outstanding.
INV-11.Early withdrawal penalty: A charge for taking money out before an agreed time, such as cashing in a certificate of deposit early or withdrawing from a retirement account too young.
INV-11.12b-1 fee: A yearly fee some mutual funds take from fund assets to pay for marketing and selling the fund. It is named after a Securities and Exchange Commission rule and is part of the expense ratio.
INV-11.Redemption fee: A charge some mutual funds apply when shares are sold soon after being bought. It is paid back into the fund to discourage rapid trading.
INV-11.Account transfer fee: A charge a brokerage makes when you move your account and its holdings to another firm or close the account.
INV-11.Inactivity fee: A charge some brokers apply to an account that makes no trades, or too few, during a set period.
INV-11.Surrender charge: A penalty for withdrawing money from an annuity or cashing in certain insurance products during the first years of the contract.
INV-11.Performance fee: A share of the profits that a hedge fund or private fund manager keeps as a reward for good results, on top of the regular management fee.
INV-11.Wrap fee: A single yearly percentage that covers advice, trading and account services together in one bundled charge.
INV-11.Markup: The amount a dealer adds to the price of a security, most often a bond, that it sells from its own holdings. It is built into the price instead of listed separately.
INV-11.Options contract fee: A small charge for each options contract traded, which many brokers apply even when they charge no commission on stocks.
INV-11.Regulatory fees: Very small charges on sales of securities that brokers pass on to customers to cover fees set by market regulators.
INV-11.Currency conversion fee: A cost of changing dollars into another currency, or back again, when buying or selling investments on a foreign market.

FIN-09.U.S. dollar: The currency of the United States. It is the most widely used currency in world trade and the one most central banks hold in reserve.
FIN-09.Euro: The shared currency of most European Union countries, including Germany, France, Italy and Spain. It is managed by the European Central Bank.
FIN-09.British pound: The currency of the United Kingdom, formally called the pound sterling. It is one of the oldest currencies still in use.
FIN-09.Japanese yen: The currency of Japan and one of the most heavily traded currencies in the world.
FIN-09.Peso: The name of the currency in Mexico and in several other countries, including the Philippines, Argentina, Chile and Colombia. Each country's peso is a separate currency.
FIN-09.Canadian dollar: The currency of Canada. It is nicknamed the loonie after the bird, a loon, shown on the one-dollar coin.
FIN-09.Chinese yuan: The currency of China. Its official name is the renminbi, and the yuan is the unit in which prices are counted.
FIN-09.Rupee: The name of the currency in India and in several nearby countries, including Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Nepal. Each country's rupee is a separate currency.
FIN-09.Swiss franc: The currency of Switzerland. Investors often treat it as a safe place to hold money in uncertain times.
FIN-09.Australian dollar: The currency of Australia. Its value is closely tied to the prices of the raw materials Australia exports.
FIN-09.Russian ruble: The currency of Russia, divided into 100 kopeks.
FIN-09.South Korean won: The currency of South Korea, one of the largest economies in Asia.
FIN-09.Brazilian real: The currency of Brazil, the largest economy in South America. Its plural is reais.
FIN-09.South African rand: The currency of South Africa. It is named after the Witwatersrand, the ridge where the country's gold was found.
FIN-09.Swedish krona: The currency of Sweden, which belongs to the European Union but has kept its own money instead of adopting the euro.
FIN-09.Turkish lira: The currency of Turkey. Lira was also the name of Italy's currency before Italy adopted the euro.
FIN-09.Saudi riyal: The currency of Saudi Arabia. Its exchange rate is held fixed against the U.S. dollar.
FIN-09.Dirham: The name of the currency in the United Arab Emirates and in Morocco. The two countries' dirhams are separate currencies.
FIN-09.Norwegian or Danish krone: Norway and Denmark each have a currency called the krone, which means crown. The two are separate currencies with different values.
FIN-09.Israeli shekel: The currency of Israel, officially called the new shekel.
FIN-09.Thai baht: The currency of Thailand, a major destination for international tourists.
FIN-09.New Zealand dollar: The currency of New Zealand, nicknamed the kiwi after the country's national bird.
FIN-09.Hong Kong dollar: The currency of Hong Kong, a major financial center. Its exchange rate is kept within a narrow band against the U.S. dollar.
FIN-09.Singapore dollar: The currency of Singapore, a small but wealthy trading and financial center in Southeast Asia.
FIN-09.Polish zloty: The currency of Poland, which belongs to the European Union but has not adopted the euro.
FIN-09.Vietnamese dong: The currency of Vietnam. One unit is worth very little, so everyday prices run into the thousands.
FIN-09.Indonesian rupiah: The currency of Indonesia, the country with the largest population in Southeast Asia.
FIN-09.Nigerian naira: The currency of Nigeria, the country with the largest population in Africa.
FIN-09.Shilling: The name of the currency in several East African countries, including Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. Each country's shilling is a separate currency.
FIN-09.Dinar: The name of the currency in a number of countries, including Kuwait, Iraq, Jordan and Serbia. Each country's dinar is a separate currency.

FIN-10.Budgeting: Working with managers to set a plan for the coming period that shows how much each part of the company expects to bring in and is allowed to spend.
FIN-10.Bookkeeping: Recording every sale, purchase, receipt and payment in the accounting records, so the company always has an accurate picture of its finances.
FIN-10.Paying bills: Checking invoices from suppliers and paying them correctly and on time. This function is called accounts payable.
FIN-10.Payroll: Calculating what each employee has earned, withholding taxes and other deductions, and making sure everyone is paid on schedule.
FIN-10.Financial reporting: Preparing the income statement, balance sheet and other statements that tell owners, lenders and managers how the company has performed.
FIN-10.Preparing taxes: Working out what the company owes in income, sales and payroll taxes, filing the returns and paying on time.
FIN-10.Billing and collections: Sending invoices to customers who bought on credit and following up until the money comes in. This function is called accounts receivable.
FIN-10.Managing cash flow: Tracking money coming in and going out so there is always enough cash to pay bills and wages when they are due.
FIN-10.Financial forecasting: Estimating future sales, costs and profits from past results and current trends, so managers can plan ahead.
FIN-10.Raising capital: Getting the money the company needs to operate and grow, by borrowing from lenders or by selling shares to investors.
FIN-10.Financial analysis: Studying the numbers, for example with ratios or by comparing actual results with the budget, to explain how the company is doing and why.
FIN-10.Cost control: Monitoring spending across the company and finding ways to keep expenses in line with the budget.
FIN-10.Investing surplus funds: Putting cash the company does not need right away into safe, short-term investments so it earns a return instead of sitting idle.
FIN-10.Capital budgeting: Evaluating large long-term spending proposals, such as a new factory or major equipment, to decide which are worth the money.
FIN-10.Internal controls: Setting up procedures, such as approvals and separation of duties, that protect the company's assets and keep its records accurate.
FIN-10.Auditing: Checking that the financial records are correct and that procedures are followed, and supplying outside auditors with what they need.
FIN-10.Risk management: Identifying financial dangers, such as uninsured losses or changes in interest rates, and arranging insurance or other protection.
FIN-10.Regulatory compliance: Making sure the company follows financial laws and reporting rules, including any filings required by government regulators.
FIN-10.Credit management: Deciding which customers may buy now and pay later, how much credit each one gets and what the payment terms are.
FIN-10.Investor relations: Communicating the company's results and plans to shareholders, financial analysts and potential investors.
FIN-10.Managing debt: Keeping track of the company's loans and bonds, making payments on time and refinancing when better terms are available.
FIN-10.Advising management: Giving executives the financial facts and analysis they need for decisions such as setting prices, expanding or cutting a product line.
FIN-10.Dividend decisions: Recommending how much of the profit should be paid out to shareholders and how much should be kept in the business.
FIN-10.Expense reimbursement: Reviewing employees' claims for business costs they paid themselves, such as travel, and paying back the approved amounts.

FIN-11.Paying a dividend: The board of directors votes to pay part of the company's profit to shareholders, usually in cash and usually every quarter.
FIN-11.Stock split: The company gives shareholders more shares for each one they hold, such as two for one. The price per share falls in proportion, so the value of a holding does not change.
FIN-11.Merger: Two companies combine into one. Shareholders of each usually vote on the deal and end up owning shares of the combined company.
FIN-11.Acquisition: One company buys another. Shareholders of the company being bought receive cash, shares of the buyer or a mix of both.
FIN-11.Stock buyback: The company uses its cash to buy its own shares on the market. Fewer shares remain, so each one represents a larger slice of the company.
FIN-11.Issuing new shares: The company sells additional stock to raise money. Each existing share then represents a smaller slice of the company, which is called dilution.
FIN-11.Initial public offering: The first sale of a company's stock to the public, which turns a private company into one whose shares trade on an exchange.
FIN-11.Spin-off: The company turns one of its divisions into a separate, independent company and hands shares of it to its existing shareholders.
FIN-11.Reverse stock split: The company combines shares, for example ten old shares into one new share, to raise the price per share. The value of a holding does not change.
FIN-11.Stock dividend: A dividend paid in additional shares of the company's stock instead of in cash.
FIN-11.Bankruptcy or liquidation: A company that cannot pay its debts reorganizes under court protection or sells its assets. Shareholders are paid last and often lose their whole investment.
FIN-11.Special dividend: A one-time payment to shareholders, on top of any regular dividend, often made after an unusually profitable period or the sale of an asset.
FIN-11.Going private: An owner or investor group buys all the publicly held shares, so the stock stops trading and the company is no longer public.
FIN-11.Delisting: The company's stock is removed from a stock exchange, either by the company's choice or because it no longer meets the exchange's requirements.
FIN-11.Changing the dividend: The board raises, cuts or suspends the regular dividend. The share price often reacts sharply because the change signals how the company expects to do.
FIN-11.Shareholder meeting and proxy vote: The company calls a meeting at which shareholders vote, in person or by proxy, on matters such as electing directors and approving mergers.
FIN-11.Rights offering: The company gives existing shareholders the right to buy new shares, usually below the market price, before anyone else can.
FIN-11.Tender offer: A public offer to buy shares directly from shareholders at a stated price, usually above the market price, for a limited time.
FIN-11.Name or ticker symbol change: The company changes its legal name or the symbol its stock trades under, often after a merger or a change of strategy.
FIN-11.Divestiture: The company sells off a division, subsidiary or major asset, which changes the business that the shareholders own.
FIN-11.Adopting a poison pill: A defense against a hostile takeover. It lets existing shareholders buy more shares cheaply if an outsider acquires a large stake, making a takeover more expensive.

ACC-09.Separation of duties: Giving related tasks to different people, so that no one person can both handle an asset and keep the records for it. Stealing would then take two people working together.
ACC-09.Audits: Examinations of the records and procedures by someone independent of the people who keep them, either the company's own internal auditors or an outside accounting firm.
ACC-09.Bank reconciliation: Comparing the company's cash records with the bank statement and explaining every difference. It reveals errors, missing deposits and unauthorized payments.
ACC-09.Locked safe or vault: A physical safeguard: cash, checks and valuable items are kept locked up, and only a few people have the key or combination.
ACC-09.Security cameras: Video monitoring of places where cash and goods are handled. It discourages theft and gives evidence if something goes missing.
ACC-09.Approval and authorization: Requiring a manager to sign off before money is spent, credit is granted or records are changed, often with a dollar limit for each level of manager.
ACC-09.Passwords and access controls: Limiting who can get into the accounting system, and what each user may see or change there, so that records cannot be altered by the wrong person.
ACC-09.Cash registers: Machines that record each sale as it happens and print a receipt. The cash in the drawer can then be checked against the register's own total.
ACC-09.Physical inventory counts: Counting the goods actually on hand and comparing the result with the inventory records, to detect theft, loss or recording mistakes.
ACC-09.Prenumbered documents: Checks, invoices and receipts printed with numbers in sequence. A missing number shows at once that a document has been lost, hidden or misused.
ACC-09.Daily bank deposits: Taking each day's cash receipts to the bank promptly, so little cash is left on the premises where it could be stolen.
ACC-09.Requiring two signatures: Making two authorized people sign a check or approve a large payment, so that no one can move money out alone.
ACC-09.Documentation and record keeping: Keeping a source document, such as an invoice or receipt, for every transaction so that each entry in the records can be traced and verified.
ACC-09.Paying by check or electronic transfer: Making payments through the bank instead of in cash, which leaves a record of who was paid, how much and when.
ACC-09.Petty cash fund: A small, fixed amount of cash kept for minor expenses. One person is responsible for it, and a slip is filled out for every payment.
ACC-09.Background checks: Looking into a job applicant's history before hiring, especially for positions that involve handling money.
ACC-09.Mandatory vacations: Requiring employees to take time off or rotate jobs. A fraud that needs constant covering up tends to surface when someone else does the work.
ACC-09.Cash counts: Counting the money in a cash drawer, often without warning, and comparing it with what the records say should be there.
ACC-09.Voucher system: A set of procedures in which every payment must be supported by an approved form, called a voucher, before a check is written.
ACC-09.Bonding employees: Buying a fidelity bond, a kind of insurance that repays the business if a covered employee steals from it.
ACC-09.Budget comparisons: Regularly comparing actual results with the budget and investigating large differences, which can point to errors, waste or fraud.
ACC-09.Lockbox system: Customers mail their payments to a post office box that the bank opens. The money goes straight into the account without passing through employees' hands.
ACC-09.Whistleblower hotline: A confidential way for employees to report suspected fraud or wrongdoing without fear of punishment.
ACC-09.Three-way match: Before a supplier is paid, the invoice is compared with the purchase order and the receiving report to confirm that the goods were ordered and actually arrived.

ACC-10.Fixed cost: A cost whose total stays the same over a period no matter how much is produced or sold, within the normal range of activity. Rent is a common example.
ACC-10.Variable cost: A cost whose total rises and falls in step with the amount produced or sold, such as the materials that go into each unit.
ACC-10.Direct cost: A cost that can be traced easily to one particular product, department or job, such as the wood used in a table.
ACC-10.Indirect cost: A cost that supports several products or departments and cannot be traced to just one, so it has to be shared out among them.
ACC-10.Overhead: All the costs of running a factory other than direct materials and direct labor, such as factory rent, utilities and supervisors' pay.
ACC-10.Opportunity cost: The benefit given up by choosing one option over the next best one. It does not appear in the accounting records but matters in decisions.
ACC-10.Direct materials: The raw materials and parts that become part of the finished product and can be traced to it.
ACC-10.Direct labor: The wages of the workers who make the product with their own hands or machines and whose time can be traced to it.
ACC-10.Sunk cost: Money already spent that cannot be recovered whatever is decided now. Because no choice can change it, it should be ignored in decisions.
ACC-10.Marginal cost: The additional cost of producing one more unit. Comparing it with the additional revenue shows whether making more is worthwhile.
ACC-10.Mixed cost: A cost with a fixed part and a variable part, such as a phone plan with a flat monthly charge plus a fee for usage. Also called a semivariable cost.
ACC-10.Total cost: The sum of all fixed costs and all variable costs at a given level of output.
ACC-10.Product cost: A cost of making a product: direct materials, direct labor and factory overhead. It is carried in inventory until the product is sold.
ACC-10.Period cost: A cost that is not part of making the product, such as selling and administrative expenses. It is recorded as an expense in the period it occurs.
ACC-10.Average cost: Total cost divided by the number of units produced. It tells you what each unit costs on average.
ACC-10.Controllable or uncontrollable cost: A controllable cost is one a particular manager has the authority to change, and an uncontrollable cost is one that manager cannot. Managers should be judged only on costs they can control.
ACC-10.Step cost: A cost that stays level over a range of activity and then jumps to a new level, such as hiring one more supervisor for every extra shift.
ACC-10.Prime cost: Direct materials plus direct labor, the costs most directly tied to making a product.
ACC-10.Conversion cost: Direct labor plus factory overhead, the costs of turning raw materials into finished products.
ACC-10.Standard cost: A carefully set estimate of what a unit should cost to make. Comparing it with the actual cost shows where the business is over or under.
ACC-10.Relevant cost: A future cost that differs between the options being compared. Only relevant costs should affect a decision.
ACC-10.Explicit or implicit cost: An explicit cost is an actual payment, such as wages or rent. An implicit cost is the value of something used without payment, such as the owner's own time.
ACC-10.Joint cost: A cost of a single process that yields two or more products at once, such as refining crude oil into gasoline and other fuels.
ACC-10.Discretionary or committed fixed cost: A discretionary fixed cost, such as advertising, can be cut by managers in the short run. A committed one, such as a lease, cannot.

ACC-11.Patent: An exclusive right, granted by the government for a limited number of years, to make, use and sell an invention.
ACC-11.Trademark: A name, logo, symbol or slogan that identifies a company or its products and that others may not legally copy.
ACC-11.Copyright: The exclusive legal right to reproduce and sell a creative work, such as a book, song, film or computer program.
ACC-11.Goodwill: The extra amount a buyer pays for a company above the fair value of its identifiable net assets. It reflects things like reputation and loyal customers.
ACC-11.Brand name: A name that customers know and trust, which lets a company sell more or charge more. It appears on the balance sheet only when bought from another company.
ACC-11.Franchise: The right to run a business under another company's name and system in a particular area, bought from the franchisor.
ACC-11.License: Permission to do something that would otherwise not be allowed, such as broadcasting on a radio frequency or using another company's technology.
ACC-11.Trade secret: Valuable information a company keeps confidential, such as a recipe, formula or process, which gives it an edge over competitors.
ACC-11.Software: Computer programs a business has bought or developed. They have value and a useful life but no physical substance.
ACC-11.Customer list: A record of who a company's customers are and how to reach them. It has value because it can be used to make future sales.
ACC-11.Domain name: A registered internet address. A short or memorable one can be worth a great deal because it brings visitors to a website.
ACC-11.Customer relationships: Established ties with customers who are expected to keep buying. A value is placed on them when one company acquires another.
ACC-11.Non-compete agreement: A contract in which a seller or former employee promises not to compete with the business for a set time, which protects its future sales.
ACC-11.Proprietary technology: Know-how, designs and processes that a company has developed and owns, whether or not they are protected by a patent.
ACC-11.In-process research and development: Unfinished research projects obtained by buying another company. They are recorded as an asset because they may lead to future products.
ACC-11.Leasehold: The right to use a property for a period under a lease. Favorable lease terms can be valuable, particularly to a company buying the business.
ACC-11.Broadcast rights: The right to show or distribute content, such as sports events, films or music, usually bought for a set period.
ACC-11.Easement: A legal right to use land owned by someone else for a specific purpose, such as running a pipeline or power line across it.
ACC-11.Contract rights: The value of agreements already in place, such as a supply contract on good terms or a backlog of customer orders waiting to be filled.
ACC-11.Emission allowances: Permits that let a company release a set amount of a pollutant. They can be bought and sold, so they have value.
ACC-11.Cryptocurrency: Digital coins such as Bitcoin held by a business. They have no physical form, so accounting rules treat them as intangible assets.

PFL-09.Scholarships: Money awarded for achievement, talent or other qualities, by colleges, companies and community groups. It does not have to be repaid.
PFL-09.Student loans: Borrowed money that must be repaid with interest after leaving school. Federal loans have fixed interest rates and more flexible repayment options than most private ones.
PFL-09.Grants: Money given mainly on the basis of financial need, by the federal government, states and colleges. The federal Pell Grant is the best known. Grants are not repaid.
PFL-09.Savings: Money the student or family set aside ahead of time. Every dollar saved is a dollar that does not have to be borrowed and repaid with interest.
PFL-09.Working a job: Earning money during the school year or over the summer and putting the wages toward tuition, books and living costs.
PFL-09.Financial aid: The overall package of grants, scholarships, work-study and loans a student is offered. Applying starts with the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA).
PFL-09.Help from parents or family: Money that parents or other relatives contribute from their income or savings. Aid formulas assume families will pay part of the cost if they can.
PFL-09.529 plan: A state-sponsored investment account for education. Earnings grow free of federal tax, and withdrawals are tax-free when spent on qualified school costs.
PFL-09.Work-study: A federal program that funds part-time jobs, often on campus, for students with financial need. The student is paid wages for hours worked.
PFL-09.Private loans: Education loans from banks, credit unions and other lenders. Approval and the interest rate depend on credit, so most students need a cosigner.
PFL-09.Military benefits: Education money earned through military service, such as the GI Bill for veterans or a Reserve Officers' Training Corps (ROTC) scholarship.
PFL-09.Employer tuition assistance: A benefit in which an employer pays for part or all of an employee's classes, often by reimbursing the cost after a course is passed.
PFL-09.Parent PLUS loans: Federal loans that parents take out in their own names to help pay for a dependent undergraduate student's education.
PFL-09.Tuition payment plan: An arrangement with the college to spread the bill for a term over several monthly payments instead of paying it all at once, usually for a small fee.
PFL-09.Education tax credits: Reductions in federal income tax, such as the American Opportunity Tax Credit, for families that paid tuition and other qualified costs.
PFL-09.Institutional aid: Grants and scholarships that come from the college's own funds, which lower the price that particular student pays.
PFL-09.Resident assistant job: A student job supervising a floor of a residence hall. It is usually paid with free or reduced housing and sometimes meals.
PFL-09.Assistantship or fellowship: Funding mostly for graduate students. An assistantship pays tuition or a stipend in return for teaching or research work, and a fellowship is an award with no work duty.
PFL-09.Crowdfunding: Raising small contributions from many people, usually through a website, to cover education costs.
PFL-09.Income share agreement: A contract in which a school or investor pays for part of a student's education in return for a set percentage of the student's income for a period after leaving.
PFL-09.Tuition waiver: A decision by the college not to charge some or all tuition to certain students, such as the children of its employees.
PFL-09.IRA withdrawals: Money taken from an individual retirement account (IRA). The usual early withdrawal penalty does not apply when it pays for qualified higher education costs, though income tax may still be due.
PFL-09.AmeriCorps education award: Money earned by completing a term of national service with AmeriCorps. It can be used for college costs or to repay student loans.
PFL-09.Savings bonds: U.S. savings bonds cashed in to pay tuition. For families who qualify, the interest can be free of federal income tax when used for higher education.

PFL-10.Gas: The fuel the car burns, or the electricity used to charge an electric car. The cost depends on how far you drive and how efficient the car is.
PFL-10.Insurance: The premium paid for auto coverage, which nearly every state requires. Young drivers usually pay the highest prices.
PFL-10.Car payment: The amount paid for the car itself: the purchase price or down payment, and then the monthly loan or lease payment if it is financed.
PFL-10.Maintenance: Routine care that keeps the car running, such as oil changes, new brake pads and scheduled service.
PFL-10.Repairs: The cost of fixing things that break or wear out unexpectedly. Repairs tend to grow more frequent and more expensive as a car ages.
PFL-10.Registration: The fee paid to the state, usually every year or two, for the legal right to drive the car on public roads and for its license plates.
PFL-10.Tires: Tires wear down with use and must be replaced every few years, which is one of the larger maintenance bills.
PFL-10.Parking: Charges for leaving the car somewhere, such as meters, garages or a school or apartment parking permit.
PFL-10.Depreciation: The drop in the car's value as it ages and is driven. You do not pay it as a bill, but you feel it when you sell or trade in the car.
PFL-10.Taxes: Sales tax when the car is bought and, in some states, a yearly property tax based on the car's value.
PFL-10.Tolls: Fees charged for using certain highways, bridges and tunnels.
PFL-10.Loan interest: The cost of borrowing to buy the car. It is included in each monthly payment and adds to the total paid over the life of the loan.
PFL-10.Car washes: The cost of keeping the car clean inside and out, which also helps protect the paint and the resale value.
PFL-10.Inspection: A fee for the safety or emissions test that many states require before a car can be registered or have its registration renewed.
PFL-10.Drivers license: The fee the state charges to issue a license to drive and to renew it every few years.
PFL-10.Traffic and parking tickets: Fines for breaking traffic or parking rules. Moving violations can also raise your insurance premium.
PFL-10.Title fee: A charge for the document that proves who owns the car, paid when ownership changes hands, often along with dealer paperwork fees.
PFL-10.Roadside assistance: A membership or add-on that pays for towing, a jump start or a flat-tire change if the car breaks down.
PFL-10.Accessories: Optional extras the owner adds, such as floor mats, a phone mount or custom wheels.
PFL-10.Extended warranty: An optional service contract that pays for certain repairs after the manufacturer's warranty has ended.
PFL-10.Insurance deductible: The part of a repair bill you pay yourself after an accident or other covered loss before the insurance pays the rest.

PFL-11.Deduction: An amount subtracted from income before the tax is figured, so less of your income is taxed.
PFL-11.Refund: Money the government sends back when more tax was withheld or paid during the year than you turned out to owe.
PFL-11.Filing status: The category that describes your household, such as single, married filing jointly or head of household. It sets your standard deduction and tax brackets.
PFL-11.Dependent: A person, usually a child or other relative you support, whom you list on your return. Having dependents can qualify you for certain credits.
PFL-11.Standard deduction: A fixed amount, set by filing status, that any taxpayer may subtract from income without listing individual expenses.
PFL-11.Tax credit: An amount subtracted directly from the tax you owe, such as the child tax credit. A credit saves more than a deduction of the same size.
PFL-11.Taxable income: The income the tax is actually figured on: adjusted gross income minus the standard deduction or itemized deductions.
PFL-11.W-2: The form an employer sends each worker after the year ends, showing wages earned and the taxes withheld from them. Its numbers go onto the tax return.
PFL-11.Form 1040: The main form individuals use to file a federal income tax return with the Internal Revenue Service.
PFL-11.Adjusted gross income: Total income minus certain specific adjustments, such as student loan interest. Many deductions and credits are limited according to this figure.
PFL-11.Itemized deductions: Specific expenses, such as mortgage interest and gifts to charity, that are listed one by one. Taxpayers itemize when the total is more than the standard deduction.
PFL-11.Withholding: Income tax an employer takes out of each paycheck and sends to the government during the year. It counts as tax already paid when you file.
PFL-11.Tax bracket: A range of income taxed at a particular rate. Rates rise from one bracket to the next, and the rate on your last dollar is your marginal tax rate.
PFL-11.Gross income: All the income you received during the year from every taxable source, such as wages, tips and interest, before anything is subtracted.
PFL-11.Tax liability: The total tax you owe for the year. Comparing it with what you already paid shows whether you get a refund or must pay more.
PFL-11.Form 1099: A family of forms that report income other than wages, such as bank interest, dividends and payments for freelance work.
PFL-11.Filing deadline: The date by which the return must be filed and any tax owed must be paid, usually in mid-April. It is often called Tax Day.
PFL-11.Capital gains: Profits from selling investments or property for more than you paid. They are reported on the return, and those on assets held over a year get lower rates.
PFL-11.Interest and dividend income: Money earned on savings accounts, bonds and stocks. It is taxable and must be reported even if it was never withdrawn.
PFL-11.Social Security number: The identification number entered on the return for the taxpayer and for each dependent, which the government uses to match its records.
PFL-11.E-file: Sending the return to the government electronically instead of mailing paper forms. It is faster and usually leads to a quicker refund.
PFL-11.Adjustments to income: Certain amounts, such as student loan interest, that are subtracted from total income to reach adjusted gross income. You can claim them without itemizing.
PFL-11.Estimated tax payments: Payments made in four installments during the year by people whose income has no withholding, such as the self-employed.
PFL-11.Amended return: A corrected return filed to fix a mistake or add something left off a return that has already been filed.
PFL-11.Self-employment income: Profit from working for yourself, reported on Schedule C. It is subject to income tax and to a separate tax that funds Social Security and Medicare.
PFL-11.Extension: Extra time to file the return, available on request. It does not give extra time to pay, so any tax owed is still due by the original deadline.
PFL-11.Alternative minimum tax: A separate tax calculation that limits some deductions so that higher-income taxpayers pay at least a minimum amount of tax.
PFL-11.Balance due: The amount you still have to pay when you file: your total tax minus what was already withheld or paid during the year. It is the opposite of a refund.
